2.content: The Java API for addon makers: add your own journal nodes, worlds, constellations, events and gate conditions with a method call, on Fabric and NeoForge.

18.content: Machines: the mod's console and Machine Cards

24.content: Client: graphics, HUD, notices, sounds, moments

26.content: The mod's catalogs from your files

28.content:
has a public Java API for addons. With it an addon adds its own content to the mod's systems with a method call —
a journal node, a world for rockets, a constellation, a world event, a gate condition, a climate zone, a whole people of natives
with your own body or a task for one, a creature with the mod's tricks and keeping, a boss with the mod's boss bar, a weapon with mastery,
a console for a machine, a spacesuit module, a substance for the spectral laboratory, a radio source, a rift or vent leading to your world,
a body in open space, a starship hull with your own model, a ship module, a station order, a HUD element or a strong moment — reads their state
and listens to their events. Some things need no API at all: they are open through the game's data (see “Open through data”), and nine catalogs of the mod take entries from your JSON files (see “The mod's catalogs from your files”). No mixins, no access wideners, no copying of the mod's logic.

29.content:
**The contract is the package `me.moltea.unbound.api`** and its subpackages. Everything else in the mod is internal and may
change in any release.

30.content:
**The API has its own version** — `UnboundApi.VERSION` (now 1.5.0, semantic versioning): a changed or removed method bumps
the major number, a new one bumps the minor number; removals are marked `@Deprecated` at least one minor version ahead.

31.content:
**The same API on Minecraft 26.3, 1.21.1 and 1.20.1**, on Fabric and NeoForge: method signatures do not change between game
versions, only the game's own types do (for example, `Identifier` on 26.3 is `ResourceLocation` on 1.21.1). Build your
addon against the mod's jar for your game version.

32.content: **Javadoc** of the package is in English; the overview is in `api/package-info.java`.

33.content:
Your own blocks, items and creatures you register the usual way, in your namespace; the API connects them to the mod's
systems by id or by supplier.

34.content:
Implement `UnboundAddon`. The mod calls `register` once per game start, on the client and on the dedicated server, before its
own lists are read — the load order of mods does not matter. Install your addon on the server and on every player, like the
mod itself.

35.content:
**Fabric** — list the class in your `fabric.mod.json` under the entrypoint key equal to the mod id (the same word as the
mod's command; in code — `UnboundApi.modId()`):

36.content:
**NeoForge** — nothing to declare: a class of your mod that directly implements `UnboundAddon` and has a public constructor
without arguments is found on its own.

38.content:
**Registrations** are static methods with the `AddonContext` as the first argument. They work only inside `register` and
with its own context; otherwise they throw `IllegalStateException`.

39.content:
**Ids.** Things are named by `Identifier`: the mod's own — `<mod id>:mars`, `<mod id>:solar_eclipse`; yours — `ctx.id("path")`.
Progress keys are strings; a journal node's id is also its progress key.

40.content:
**Texts** of your content are translation keys in your namespace (listed in each section below). Without a translation the
mod shows the path in words, not a raw key.

41.content:
**Events** are fields of the `<Area>Events` class of each area. They fire on the server, once per happening; an event nobody
listens to costs nothing.

42.content:
**Energy, fluids and items** of machines go through the loaders' own standards (Team Reborn Energy and Fabric Transfer on
Fabric, capabilities on NeoForge) — see “Compatibility”. There is no separate API for them.

43.content: Package `api.journal`. Your own chapter and nodes of the star journal; goals; checking and granting progress keys.

44.content: A chapter becomes a tab after the mod's own; a node's place on the canvas is laid out by its links, like the mod's nodes.

45.content:
Goals: `granted()` (your code grants it), `item`, `items`, `key`, `either`, `alone`, `custom` (checked once a second while
the node is open).

46.content: Queries on the server: `Journal.has`, `Journal.grant`, `Journal.state`; on the client — `ClientJournal.has`.

49.content:
Package `api.travel`. A destination for your dimension: rockets, the End shuttle or the Nether bell fly there, land and
return like on the mod's worlds; on the space road it has a ball on the star map and, if you wish, in the Solar System for
starships.

50.content: The dimension itself (generator, dimension type with gravity, air and heat) is your own data.

51.content: A destination with a discovery key stays hidden until the player has the key; grant it from your code, a journal node or the sky.

53.content:
Events: `LAUNCH`, `LANDING` (with a first-landing flag), `SHIP_TRAVEL` (a starship leaves or enters a world, jumps, takes
a far road or an interstellar jump).

54.content:
Texts and pictures: name `destination.<namespace>.<path>` and `….facts`; surface map `textures/space/<path>.png`;
shuttle and bell window sprite `passage/<path>`.

55.content: Package `api.sky`. Your own constellation, body (moon, planet) or deep-sky sight (nebula, cluster, galaxy) in the telescope sky.

56.content: A body or a sight may wait for keys (`requires`); a completed constellation grants your keys (`grants`).

57.content: Queries: `hasCompleted`, `hasDiscovered`, progress keys, lists of all constellations and bodies.

60.content:
Package `api.sky`. Your own rift in the sky of the End and vent in the magma of the Nether. Players find them with the mod's riftscope and
magmascope exactly like the mod's eight — follow the void sparks and tear the seam, strike the magma and crack the crust in time with
its pulse — and the world behind them is your destination of the shuttle or bell road.

61.content:
Rifts hang 20–82° above the horizon, vents lie 15–82° below it; keep clear of the mod's (azimuths 55, 165, 250, 330 and 40, 130, 225,
310) — a place too close is refused at `register()`.

62.content:
`leadsTo` takes a destination of the same road (`Craft.RIFT_SHUTTLE` for a rift, `Craft.DIVING_BELL` for a vent); finding the place grants
the destination's discovery key. `fromStage(n)` waits for the End or Nether stage; `requires` and `grants` work like in the sky.

64.content:
Texts: `sky_rift.<namespace>.<path>` (`.facts`, `.clue`), `sky_vent.<namespace>.<path>`; pictures — GUI sprites
`observatory/rift/<path>`, `observatory/vent/<path>` and `<path>_crust` in your namespace.

65.content: Your places do not change the stages of the End and the Nether — count them yourself with `Stages.advance` if you want to.

66.content:
Package `api.worldevent`. A rare world event or a weather in any world — the mod's, yours or a vanilla one — built from
ready-made effects (sky and fog color, daylight, particles, wind, hail, falling items, swarms, sounds) and your own code.

67.content:
Environment effects take the attribute by its id, the same on every Minecraft version the mod supports:
`Effects.scale(Identifier.withDefaultNamespace("visual/fog_end_distance"), Effects.Op.MULTIPLY, 0.4F)`, `tint`, `recolor`, `flag`
(API 1.1.0). The older forms with the game's `EnvironmentAttribute` type exist only on Minecraft 26.x and are deprecated.

68.content: Your own effect runs once every `every` ticks and only while players are there.

69.content: The mod's commands start and stop your event by id: `<command> event <namespace>:<path>`.

72.content: **Meteorites (API 1.5.0).** `Meteors.kinds()`, `Meteors.drop(level, player, kind, size, natural)` and `Meteors.dropAt(...)` drop a meteorite of a kind and size; event: `MeteorEvents.LANDED`.

74.content:
Package `api.awaken`. The Nether and the End change for the whole server as players find rifts and vents (stages 0–4, see
The Nether and the End). Read the stage, react to its change, add events and weathers that come only from a
stage on, and count your own content toward it.

75.content:
Queries: `Stages.stage(level)` and `reached(level, n)` on both sides; on the server also `stage(server, Level.END)`, `enabled`,
`opened` (found rifts or vents as ids), `places`, `name`. Client only: `ClientStages`.

76.content:
`fromStage(n)` (1–4) only for events and weathers of the Nether or the End; below the stage the schedule waits. The mod's commands still
start them at any stage.

77.content: `STAGE_CHANGED` fires once per change of the shown stage: growth, the `stage` command, the owner's switch.

78.content: `Stages.advance(level, n, player)` raises the world to at least stage `n`, with the mod's notice and moment; it only grows.

79.content: If the server owner turned the changes off, every query answers stage 0 and stage-bound events and weathers do not come.

80.content:
Packages `api.gate` and `api.creature`. Your own condition for waking the gates of any world; a gates rule for your own world;
boss events and creature tags.

81.content: Conditions add up: the gates wake when all of them are met. Your condition is a line in the gates window with a check mark.

84.content: Tags: `acid_immune` — acid does not burn the creature; `c:bosses` — the common tag for bosses.

85.content:
Package `api.creature`. Your own creature — any `Mob` class of your addon: a `Sheep` or `Pig` subclass with the game's renderer,
a GeckoLib creature — gets the mod's tricks, keeping and a page in the Atlas of Life without extending any class of the mod.
Register the entity type yourself; describe the species by the same id with `Species.add`, then connect three hooks in your class.

86.content:
**Tricks**: nine kinds (`BREATH`, `COIL`, `LOB`, `RAM`, `DIVE`, `LUNGE`, `HOWL`, `POUNCE`, `SLAM`) with a fair warning — a glow
at the mouth, a mark on the ground — then the blow and a rest; they start only at a target your creature already has.

87.content:
**Keeping**: taming by trust (sit and follow on the owner's empty hand, let go by sneaking with the food in the other hand),
shearing with regrowth (and regrowth food), healing food, breeding (an `Animal`) only under its own sky and not when crowded.
The mod saves the state with the creature and tells the client "sheared, tamed, sitting".

88.content:
**Atlas of Life**: met, studied (watched at work for half a minute), sample (its part in the inventory), tamed, bred — each
player's own; a right click with the Star Journal opens its card. Texts: `entity.<ns>.<path>`, `creature.<ns>.<path>.lore`.

89.content:
**Queries and events**: `Species.sheared/tamed/sitting/owner`, `hasMet/hasStudied/hasSample/hasTamed/hasBred`,
`HusbandryEvents.TAMED`, `SHEARED`, `BRED`, `STUDIED` — for the mod's creatures too.

90.content: Not open: mounts, herds, sleep and hunting (behavior of the mod's own creature class).

91.content:
Packages `api.creature` and `api.dungeon`. Make your creature — your own class or a game one — a boss of the mod: the ornamental bar
with phases, hints and attack warnings, invulnerable phase transitions, the victory key, the summon at the mod's dungeon altar.
Your boss keeps its own AI and attacks; beams and particles of the mod's bosses are yours to use.

92.content:
**Phases**: the first at `1.0`, the next at lower shares of health; each has a color, a hint under the bar and, if you like, a strong
moment. Entering a phase, the boss is invulnerable for `transition(ticks)` (30) and flashes in its color.

93.content:
**Bar**: `BossBar.borrow("<mod boss>")` takes the art of one of the mod's bosses; `BossBar.own(id, phases, compact)` — your sprites
`<path>_frame_<n>`, `_fill_<n>`, `_end_left_<n>`, `_end_right_<n>`, `_crest_<n>` in your GUI atlas. `guard()` — a lair guardian
(compact bar, key `elite/<addon>:<path>`).

94.content: **Attack warnings**: `attack(name, text)` in the description, `Bosses.warn(boss, name)` at the start of the wind-up.

95.content:
**Arrows**: like the mod's masters and guardians, your boss takes only part of projectile damage and, after a streak of hits,
turns projectiles back for three seconds (a ring of shield, a blow up close breaks it). By default — as a mod boss of the same rank
and flight (master 0.6 and 6 hits, guardian 0.5 and 5, flying 0.75 and 8 / 0.6 and 6); your own numbers — `projectiles(share, volley)`,
`projectiles(1.0, 0)` turns it off.

96.content: **Victory**: every player who hit the boss or was its target gets `Bosses.victoryKey(id)` = `boss/<addon>:<path>`.

97.content:
**Altar**: put the Master's Altar `<mod id>:boss_altar` in your structure with `Dungeons.altarData(boss, offering, count, group)`
and Sealed Stones `<mod id>:sealed_stone` with `{group:"…"}` (or `Dungeons.placeAltar` / `placeSeal` from code). A player with the
offering calls your boss; the arena mechanisms of the group wake, and when the boss falls the seals crumble. `Dungeons.openSeals`
opens them from your own puzzle.

100.content: Not open: the mod's attacks and walking of its bosses, your own beam kinds, the gate heart of a master.

101.content: Package `api.gear`: your own weapon abilities and perks, weapons and artifacts with the mod's logic, armor sets of your items.

102.content:
`Gear.addAbility(ctx, path, ability)` and `Gear.addPerk(ctx, path, perk)` add kinds by id; a weapon or an artifact may also use the
mod's kinds (`<mod id>:wave`, `<mod id>:effect`) with its own numbers.

103.content:
`Gear.weapon(spec, properties)` and `Gear.artifact(spec, properties)` return a ready `Item` of the mod's class — register it yourself
(Fabric: in `register`; NeoForge: your `DeferredRegister`, because `register` runs after the registries). It gets the ability on its
trigger with a cooldown, mastery levels that change the numbers, the gear tooltip, "Hold [G]" and the details screen.

104.content:
The model is a usual item model of your namespace. Texts: `gear.<ns>.<path>.role`, `.ability`, `.ability.desc`, `.level.<n>`,
`.effect` (artifact), `gear.<ns>.world.<origin>`, `item.<ns>.<path>.lore`.

105.content: An artifact goes into Trinkets and Curios slots through one tag: `<mod id>:artifact_slot/necklace` (`ring`, `belt`, `back`).

106.content: `Gear.addArmorSet(ctx, path, spec)` gives your armor items set tiers (perks and bonuses for 2–4 pieces).

107.content:
**Modular armor (API 1.5.0).** `Gear.module(ModuleSpec, properties)` makes an armor module (places, weight, group, perks, bonuses, home worlds) — register the item yourself; the Module Bench fits it by the
mod's rules. `Gear.addSocketed(ctx, predicate, SocketedItem)` gives sockets (up to four) to your own items. Queries: `sockets`, `fittedModules`, `wornModules`, `fitModule`, `worldHarmShield`; event:
`GearEvents.MODULE_FITTED`. World harm is open as damage types `<mod id>:world_heat|cold|acid|radiation|void` and the tag `<mod id>:world_harm`.

109.content: Not open: a GeckoLib model of the mod for your weapon, the mod's own armor class.

110.content:
Package `api.natives`. Your own peoples of natives, your own tasks for any people (parcels, personal goods), topics of talk and trade
offers; what a player has with a people; task and trade events. Package `api.ringwright`: let your puzzle or fight be the trial of a Ringwright niche.

111.content:
A people is the id of its creature (`"lunarian"`, `Natives.peoples()`), a job is a string (`"elder"`). A task is an
`Identifier`: `<addon>:<people>/<path>`.

112.content:
Your task works like ours: the "!" and "?" over the native's head, the task card in the talk, the Tasks window (F7), the corner
tracker, the trust of the people. Goals: `bring`, `have`, `slay`, `key`, `counted` (your code calls `Natives.advance`),
`check` (your own test). Rewards: `item`, `xp`, `learn`, `discount`, `custom`. Texts: `quest.<addon>.<people>.<path>.title`,
`.brief`, `.offer`, `.waiting`, `.ready`, `.done`.

113.content:
A topic's question goes into the people's "What's new?" (or `under(...)` another topic); its answer has nested topics, "back"
and "farewell". Texts: `topic.<addon>.<path>.ask`, `.text`.

114.content: A trade offer joins the native's offers when the native reaches that level of its job.

117.content: `Ringwrights.pass(player, tablet)` grants `trial/<tablet>`: a niche with the `trial` condition then gives its tablet.

118.content:
Since API 1.4.0 an addon adds a whole people of natives with its own body: your GeckoLib model, texture and animations, your
jobs, a chief and named masters, lines of talk and trades. Its natives live like the mod's peoples — the mod's talk window with a
live portrait, the trade window in the people's color, the "!" and "?" marks, tasks and trust, the Jade tooltip and the "Trades" page
of JEI and REI. Tasks may now send a parcel to another people (yours or the mod's) and reward personal goods.

119.content:
The body: the model `<addon>:native/<path>` and the texture `<addon>:textures/native/<path>.png` by default. On 26.3 the files are
`geckolib/models/native/…` and `geckolib/animations/native/…`, on 1.21.1 and 1.20.1 — `geo/native/…` and `animations/native/…`; ship
both to support all three. The model stands at the origin facing north, with a head bone and the animations `idle`, `move`, `talk`,
`work`, `greet`, `trade`.

120.content:
The talk: without your own nodes the people gets the mod's plain talk — greeting, news (your topics go there), the job's node with
trading, farewell. Texts are keys `native.<addon>.<path>.greeting`, `.again`, `.news`, `.news.ask`, `.farewell`, `.craft_<job>`,
`.people`, `.job.<job>`; add lines with conditions (`NativeCondition.persona`, `job`, `firstMeeting`) or whole nodes (`dialog`).

121.content:
In the world: `Natives.spawn(level, pos, people, job, talkative)`, a command or your own structure — the entity is
`<mod id>:addon_native` with the data `people`, `job`, `talkative`. A settlement of your people is your own structure; the mod's
villages stay the mod's.

122.content:
A parcel: `NativeQuestGoal.deliver(item, count, people, job)` with `.given()` (the giver hands it over) and `.replies(...)` — what the
recipient says. Personal goods: `NativeQuestReward.goods(job, offer)` — one more trade for this player only while trading.

123.content: The same in your `natives.json`: a new people (an entry in your namespace with `jobs` and `body`), and `trades` and `topics` for any people.

124.content: Package `api.life`. Is there air, how hot it is, what gravity an entity feels, what the spacesuit holds — and changing them.

126.content:
Modifiers (`OXYGEN_USE`, `CLIMATE`, `GRAVITY`) are chained: each listener gets the value of the previous one. `GRAVITY` runs
on both sides — decide only by what both the client and the server see (held item, armor, effects).

127.content:
Places: a sphere of your own gravity, climate rules of a dimension; your own air source block (`holdAirSphere`,
`holdRoomAir`) keeps air like the mod's Oxygen Dome or Air Blower.

129.content:
Your own torso module in one call: your item fits the four torso slots on the mod's Suit Rack, like the mod's modules, and the suit
counts it wherever it counts its own. The item is a plain item of your addon, registered by you.

130.content:
Spec: `oxygen`, `charge` (suit capacity), `reserve` (own store in the module stack: `ENERGY` or `OXYGEN` from the rack, or `NONE`),
`protects` (`HEAT`, `COLD` with a share — the mod's Cooling Unit gives 0.4; `ACID`, `RADIATION` fully), `drain` (cost every N
ticks while it protects), `tick` (your action every N ticks, server), `hud`.

132.content: Events: `LifeEvents.MODULE_SPENT` (the reserve ran dry; the wearer sees a notice), `MODULE_FILLED` (the rack filled it up).

133.content:
Package `api.machine`. Energy, fluids and items of your machine still go through the loaders' standards (Team Reborn Energy and
Fabric Transfer, NeoForge capabilities). On top of them you get the mod's **console window** for your block entity — describe the
layout, the mod draws it (sockets, gauge arcs, channels, buttons, readouts, the glass inventory shelves, refusals and hints, Mouse
Tweaks, JEI and REI, the *Mod window size* setting) — and **sockets for the mod's Machine Cards** with the mod's own multipliers.

134.content:
`Consoles.menuType(layout)` is a factory: register the menu type in your own registry together with your blocks (Fabric —
`onInitialize`, NeoForge — your `DeferredRegister`). Open it with `Consoles.open(player, machine, menuType)` on the server.

135.content:
Your block entity implements `ConsoleMachine`: a `Container` plus `value(index)` (numbers the console shows), `pressed(player,
button)` and `title()`. Texts are keys of your namespace: `gui.<ns>.press.energy`, `gui.<ns>.press.progress` …

136.content: `UpgradeSlots` is used twice: in the layout (`.upgrades(CARDS)`) and in your tick (`factor`, `energyUse`).

137.content:
`MachineRecipes` feeds your items to the Fuel Plant, Pearl Liquefier, Cryo Still and Melt Pump. The Crusher and the Zero-G Forge
take data-pack recipes (`<mod id>:crushing`, `<mod id>:crushing_by_tag`, `<mod id>:zero_g_forging`) — no code at all.

138.content: `MachineRecipes.addReactorFeed` adds bioreactor feed in code; without code it is data: the item tags `<mod id>:oxygen_feed/scant|poor|fair|good|rich|lush` or an `<mod id>:oxygen_feed` recipe.

139.content:
Not open: the mod's resonance network (beams), machine kinds and Mk tiers — your machine joins the network through a mod machine
next to it (a Battery Block, an Energy Converter).

140.content:
Package `api.spectral`. Your own reference (a substance with real lines), sample, light of a sky body, recipe that only an analysis
unlocks, ore for the ore scanner and creature weakness — in the same spectral laboratory and spectrograph as the mod's.

141.content:
Lines are real: wavelengths in air from a reference (NIST ASD), strength 3 (main), 2 (strong), 1 (weak). Register references
before the samples that use them; the mod's are `<mod id>:na`, `ca`, `fe`, `h`, `co2`… (`Spectral.references()`).

142.content:
Samples burn in the arc (bright lines); gas and ice go under the lamp (`absorption()`). With `reward(...)` an identified sample is
cracked open by the laboratory.

143.content: The light of a body is registered under the body's id: your `Sky.body`, your travel destination, a body of another addon.

144.content:
Every registration is checked like the mod's catalog: no laboratory can take the sample, another reference fits its spectrum,
the ruler fits off its place — a `WARN` line in the log tells what to fix.

147.content:
Package `api.radio`. Add your own radio sources. A **pulsar** beats as dashes or ripples on the waterfall and is caught by *folding* (the player finds its
period); a **quasar** shows hydrogen and hydroxyl lines shifted by its redshift and is caught by the *template* comb. Place it in
galactic (`galactic(l, b)`) or equatorial (`equatorial(ra, dec)`) coordinates — the real sky decides where it rises (Earth 40° N, Moon
30° S, orbit sees everything; the dish stops at 12°). By default it is always on the air; `daily(from, ticks)` and `everyDays(n)`
make a schedule of world time. The first record gives your keys, items and stardust, and can give the spectrograph the light of a
body of `api.spectral` (`light`) or a navigation record of a place among the stars (`navigationRecord`). Keep sources 10° apart.

148.content:
Texts: `radio.<ns>.source.<path>` (name) and `radio.<ns>.source.<path>.found` (a line on the record card). Queries: `Radio.sources()`,
`signal`, `foundKey`, `hasFound`, `isOnAir`, `isAboveFloor`. "Wow!" and fast radio bursts stay the mod's own.

149.content:
Package `api.space` (API 1.2.0). Bodies in the Solar System, events of open space, whole spaces of your own with passages
between them, and places among the stars for the interstellar drive.

150.content:
**A body** is a ball like the mod's planets: on an orbit, at a point or next to another body (a moon); a surface map, a tilt,
a day, an atmosphere rim, rings. It is drawn on the sky, named on the ship's instruments, listed on the system map, starships
aim at it, jump to it, fly up to it and stop at its surface. It may stay hidden until found (`discovery`: the scanner or flying
up to it reveals it), lead into the sky of your travel destination (`lands`) or into another space (`passage`).

151.content:
**A space event** is scheduled like a world event in the space dimension (banner, `event` command) and adds light at its source
(`glow`), a spreading wave (`wave`) and an action on starships every few ticks; the wave reaches each ship once.

152.content:
**A space of your own** works like the Solar System: sealed cabins, the starry sky with the balls of its bodies, instruments,
scanner, jump drive, autopilot, system map. The dimension is your data (the mod's dimension type `solar_system` is the simplest).
Ships get there through a passage or by rising from the sky of your world whose ball stands there. Light comes from the middle
of the space: put your star there.

153.content:
**A place among the stars** appears on the drive's map «Interstellar» with its navigation record — a photo of your sky sight or
a key you grant (`recordKey()`); the drive jumps there with its own price by light-years; its sky is a nebula of two tones with
its own stars. Thirteen places for all addons; the place has no blocks of its own.

154.content: Starships (`Ships`): hull, fuel, a blow to the hull, a kick.

156.content:
Events (`SpaceEvents`): `SPACE_EVENT_STARTED`, `SPACE_EVENT_ENDED` (every event of every space), `BODY_DISCOVERED`,
`BODY_REACHED`; a passage is the ship leg `PASSAGE` of `TravelEvents.SHIP_TRAVEL`.

157.content:
Texts: `space_body.<namespace>.<path>` with `.facts` and `.near`; `space.<namespace>.<path>`; `event.<namespace>.<path>.name|hint`;
`star_place.<namespace>.<path>` with `.kind`, `.about`, `.find`, `.star.<id>`. Surface map — `textures/space/<path>.png`.

158.content: Not open yet: anomalies of the codex, far roads, belts and stations of your own.

159.content: `api.space` also opens the ship's module sockets, the order boards of the peoples' stations and the observatory of your own station.

160.content:
**Ship module** — `Ships.addModule(ctx, ShipModuleSpec.of(itemId)…)`. The item is yours (register it yourself); it goes into the general
module sockets. Multipliers on top of the mod's modules: `speed`, `turn`, `hull`, `tank`, `scanner`, `jump`, `jumpCost`, `shield`, and
`hold(cells)`; `kind(…)` makes tiers exclusive, `stacks(true)` lets several stand together. `flight(every, action)` runs your code on
the server every ≥ 10 ticks while the ship has a pilot. The ship window lists what the module changes under the item's tooltip.

161.content:
**Station order** — `Stations.addOrder(ctx, new StationOrderSpec(path)…)`: `bring(item, count)` and/or `task((player, takenAt) -> …)`,
`people(…)`, `in(space)`, `gate(trust step)`, `reward(supply, emeralds, trust)`, `gift(…)`, `grants(key)`. Texts:
`station.<ns>.order.<path>` and `.goal`.

162.content:
**Observatory project** — `Stations.addResearch(ctx, new ResearchSpec(path)…)`: `road`, `minutes`, `knows(count, keys…)`,
`anomalies(count, ids…)`, `cost(item, count)`, `result(item)`, `recipes(ids…)`. When done: the key `Stations.researchKey(id)` and the
recipes (the crafting table refuses them before). Texts: `research.<ns>.<path>.name|gives|story|data.<n>|data.<n>.hint`.

164.content:
Since API 1.3.0 an addon adds its own starship — a hull with its own model. You bring the look (a GeckoLib model, texture and animations
in your namespace); the mod does the rest: flight over worlds and in space, crossings, jumps, assembly on the shipyard, classes C to S,
modules, hold, deck, instruments, autopilot, the call beacon and rescue.

165.content:
**Registration** — `Ships.addForm(ctx, ShipFormSpec.of(path)…)` returns `<ns>:<path>`. `road` (`space`, `rift`, `vent`: fuel, repair
and class upgrades are the road's), `role` (`scout`, `hauler`, `explorer`, `fighter`, `exotic`). Numbers start from one of the mod's
forms — `like("swift")` — and every setter overrides one: `size`, `seat`, `eye`, `camera`, `seats`, `atmosphere`/`space` flight,
`hull`, `tank`, `hold`, `jump`, `scanner`, `slots`, `weapons` with `guns`, `engine`, `accent`, `nozzles`, `lights`, `beam`, `abilities`, `build`.

166.content:
**Shipyard** — the form appears in the list of its road. `node(item, count)` sets what it takes, `unlock(key…)` — after which progress
keys the shipyard knows it (otherwise the rule of its role, a blueprint `Ships.blueprint(form)` or creative mode).

167.content:
**Look** — your files, by game version (the mod does not move them; an addon for all three versions may ship both layouts at once,
the extra one does nothing). The ids in `ShipFormSpec` stay the same: the mod looks them up in its own GeckoLib layout.

171.content:
The front faces north, bones `gear_*`, `flame_*`,
`light_*` and `part_0…5` (assembly order) are driven by name. `cockpit("swift")` borrows a cockpit of the mod around the pilot's eye,
`deck("swift")` — its deck. Name: `ship.<ns>.<path>`, lore: `.lore`.

172.content: **Queries**: `Ships.forms()`, `isForm`, `form(ship)`, `knows(player, form)`, `stack(form)` — the ship as an item.

173.content: **Closed**: own flight physics and own weapon kinds — the form gives numbers, weapon hardpoints and gun muzzles; the guns are the mod's.

174.content: Packages `api.client` (client only, except the registration `Hud.add`), `api.notice`, `api.sound` and `api.moment` (both sides).

175.content:
**Mod graphics** — `ModGraphics.level()`, `particles(n)`, `cues(n)`, `post()`, `layers(n)`, `glow()`, `far(blocks)`, `shaderPack()`: your
effects get lighter together with the mod's when the player lowers the setting. Never thin out warnings. Low, Medium and High are
presets over knobs the player may tune one by one: `preset()` is empty for Custom, `shake()` is the share of camera shake to multiply
yours by, `cinema()` tells whether the camera may leave the player's eyes for a short film (API 1.3.0).

176.content:
**HUD** — `Hud.add(ctx, path, HudZone, order, () -> new MyElement())`: each frame your element asks the mod's HUD layout for room and
draws where it is placed — never over the mod's elements or the game's (hotbar, chat, boss bars, toasts). Sizes and the slot are in
ordinary GUI coordinates; a short form (`compactWidth/Height`) is used when space is tight. Pass the element as a lambda, not as
`MyElement::new`: then a dedicated server never loads its class.

177.content:
**Notices** — `Notices.send(player, NoticeKind.DONE, text)`, `hold(...)` for something that lasts, `progress(player, text, done, total)`
with a bar; from the server or the client. `ClientNotices.show(...)` from client-only code.

178.content:
**Sounds** — `Sounds.play(level, except, at, source, lead, volume, pitch, layers...)`: your subtitled lead plus game recordings as
layers without their subtitles (`Sounds.layer`). `Sounds.aircraft(ctx, "engine")` / `atmosphere(ctx, "ambient")` put your events under
the mod's sound switches.

180.content:
Some of the mod opens without the API, through your addon's ordinary data files (`data/<namespace>/…`), like vanilla types.
Write the mod's ids literally — `<mod id>:…` (`UnboundApi.modId()`); fields follow the game version your addon is built for.

181.content:
**Structure types** (`worldgen/structure/<id>.json`): `<mod id>:settled` — a one-template building that stands level and in
sight: the type picks the spot, the turn and the height (fields of the game's jigsaw plus `max_relief`, `search`, `ground`,
`foot` — `[x, z]` points the building stands on, `overhead` — `[x, z, height]` points the ground must not reach, `level`,
`above`, `span` for a bridge, `gorge`, `upright`, `sole`, `cave`); `<mod id>:settled_village` — a jigsaw village whose square
looks for flat ground (`max_relief`, `search`, `radius`, `above`, `below`, `level`); `<mod id>:deep_dungeon` — a many-story
dungeon on a grid of cells (`layout`).

182.content:
**Density functions** (15) for the noise settings of your dimension, next to vanilla ones. With parameters, for terrain of
your own: `craters`, `rays` (craters with ejecta rays), `facets`, `honeycomb`, `iris`, `ribs`, `lineae`, `cells`, `drift`.
Without parameters (they repeat the mod's own places): `asteroids`, `wanderer_region`, `stellar`, `weave`, `deep`, `geode`.

183.content:
**Machine recipes** (`recipe/`): the Crusher — `<mod id>:crushing` (`ingredient`, `result`, `time`) and `<mod id>:crushing_by_tag`
(`from`, `to` — tag prefixes such as `c:raw_materials` → `c:dusts`, `count`); the Zero-G Forge — `<mod id>:zero_g_forging`
(`ingredients` — up to four `{ingredient, count}`, `result`, `time`, `colors`, `key` — a progress key the recipe needs).
JEI and REI show them on the mod's pages by themselves.

184.content:
**Dungeon puzzles and the Ringwright niche in your templates** — the mod's blocks with their memory in the block entity data
of the template: `sealed_stone`, `keystone_socket`, `rune_plate_1…4` and `rune_sign_1…4`, `beam_emitter`, `mirror_a`/`mirror_b`,
`beam_receiver`, `boss_altar` (memory `group`, `order`, `key`, `boss` — only the mod's bosses, `offering`, `offeringCount`;
a solved puzzle opens the seals of its group within 48 blocks), `dungeon_treasury` (`loot` — a loot table),
`ringwright_niche` (`tablet`, `key` — `trial` waits for `Ringwrights.pass`, or any progress key).

185.content:
**Trades** of the mod's villagers and natives are the game's `villager_trade` and `trade_set` data
(`trade_set/<profession>/level_<n>.json`, `trade_set/native/<people>/<job>/level_<n>.json` in the mod's namespace): a data pack
replaces a whole file; to add one offer to a native, use `Natives.addTrade`.

186.content: **The Hydroponic Bed** grows any `CropBlock` or `StemBlock` — your crop needs nothing registered.

187.content: The mod's particles, sounds and effects are in the game's registries by id; tags — `LifeTags` and `CreatureTags` above.

188.content:
Nine catalogs of the mod also take entries from plain JSON files in your addon's jar. A file looks like the mod's own catalog,
sits at the same path, in your namespace: `assets/<namespace>/natives.json` (peoples of your own, tasks, trades and topics), `spectral.json`
(standards, samples, light of bodies, recipes after analysis, ores for the scanner, weaknesses, rewards), `research.json`
(observatory projects) and `moments.json` (strong moments); and the catalogs the mod builds blocks and items from — `ores.json`, `families.json` (stone families), `flora.json` (plants and food), `decor.json` and `gear.json` (weapons).

189.content:
The mod reads them itself, once per launch, right after every addon's `register`, on the server and on the client alike. Entries
get the same checks and land in the same lists as the Java calls (`Natives.addQuest`, `Spectral.*`, `Stations.addResearch`,
`Moments.add`), so a file may refer to what your Java code registered. The log line `Addon data <namespace>: natives.json 1, …`
tells how many entries came from each file.

190.content:
Only the namespaces of addons are read — a mod with an `UnboundAddon` entry point. A data-only addon needs one empty `register`.
Other mods' files with the same name are about their own things and are left alone.

191.content:
Not through data packs. Both sides read these catalogs from their jars and the network carries only ids. A file that only the
server had would disagree with the client, which draws the task card, the spectrum window, the observatory and the moment.

192.content:
Ids: a new entry is a path (your namespace is put before it) or `<namespace>:path`. A reference to a catalog entry works as in the
mod's file: without a namespace it is the mod's (`"s"` is the mod's sulfur, `"lunarian"` the mod's people), with one it is anyone's
(your own is `"myaddon:sr"`). Items, blocks, creatures and recipes are game ids.

193.content:
A broken entry does not stop the game. The log gets an ERROR `Addon <namespace>: <file> — <entry> skipped: <reason>`, and the rest
of the file still loads.

194.content:
Ores, families, plants and food, decor and weapons are read while the mod registers its blocks, before any `register`. The mod
finds addons without creating their classes, and registers your entries **with its own code, in your namespace**: the block, its
item, the mod's creative tab. Creatures, ships, dungeon sets and armor stay closed to files: they need the mod's GeckoLib
models and code. For them, use your own registration plus the API (`Species.add`, `Bosses.register`, `Ships.addModule`,
`Gear.addArmorSet`).

195.content:
A task in `natives.json` needs only `id` and `goals`. By default, `giver` is `*` (any member of the people), `repeat` is 0 and
the texts are keys `quest.<namespace>.<people>.<id>.title|brief|offer|waiting|ready|done`. Outside the mod the task is
`<namespace>:<people>/<id>`.

196.content:
`research.json` holds `{"projects": [{"id", "road", "minutes", "color", "result", "recipes", "data", "items"}]}`, and
`moments.json` holds `{"moments": {"<name>": {"duration": …, "beams": […], …}}}`. Both use the same fields as the mod's own files
and the Java builders above.

197.content:
The mod registers the block or item, but its data is yours, in your namespace. The mod's generators only write the mod's own
namespace.

198.content:
Blockstates, block and item models (on 26.x `items/<path>.json`), textures and `lang`: `block.<ns>.<path>`, `item.<ns>.<path>`,
and `.lore` for a description line.

199.content: Block loot tables (`data/<ns>/loot_table/blocks/<path>.json`) — without one a block drops nothing.

200.content:
Tags: `mineable/pickaxe`, `needs_iron_tool`, `c:ores`, `c:raw_materials/<x>`. With the last one, the Crusher's
`crushing_by_tag` crushes your raw ore on its own.

202.content:
Ore veins: your `configured_feature` and `placed_feature`. To add them to biomes, the mod's ones included, use a NeoForge biome
modifier (`neoforge:add_features`) or Fabric's `BiomeModifications.addFeature`.

203.content:
On 1.21.1 and 1.20.1, the render layer of plants and glass: `render_type` in the model on NeoForge and Forge, or
`BlockRenderLayerMap` on Fabric.

204.content:
An ore's `raw` and `product` are new items (a path) or an existing item by full id (`minecraft:raw_iron`). A weapon uses one of
the mod's abilities and mastery, with your own item model. Its texts are `gear.<ns>.<path>.role|ability|ability.desc`.

206.content: Five tabs of advancements: conditions and rewards.

341.content: Spoiler — open the page to read

342.content: The star journal — the path by stages.

373.content: The anomaly codex: real phenomena of space — what science knows about them, what they do in the game and where the game took liberties.

378.content: The mod's bosses: phases, attacks, fight hints, the altar offering and the reward. Mechanics are described in full — the story is not spoiled.

379.content: Masters and guardians take only part of the damage from projectiles — arrows, tridents, potions: a master 60%, a guardian 50% (flying ones 75% and 60%). After six hits in a row (a guardian — five, flying ones — eight and six) it turns arrows back for three seconds — a ring of shield flares around it; a blow up close breaks the defense. While a boss heals, a projectile goes through in full: you can break the healing from afar. Abilities of the mod's weapons (bolts, beams, the String Bow's reflection) are not projectiles: the defense does not touch them.

414.content: Creatures of the worlds: health, damage, where they live and what they drop. Masters and guardians are on the “Bosses” page.

416.content: Which mods the mod works well with: recipe viewers, tooltips, Sodium and Iris, energy and tags.

419.content: Energy and fluids of other mods

429.content:
All of the mod’s recipes are visible in the viewer: the crafting table and furnaces, the mod’s machines (crusher, melt
pump, zero-g forge, cryo-distiller, shipyard…), altar offerings and gate awakening. Items without a recipe have a “where
to get it” page: loot, creatures, caches, trades, tasks. Items that come in variants — ship blueprints, Ringwright
tablets, Orphan Records, copper patina stages — are listed in the viewer one by one. JEI and REI work on both loaders.

430.content:
The **Trades** page gathers everything the mod’s creatures exchange: the natives of every world and the Earth villagers
of the mod (by craft and level), personal goods unlocked by tasks, a cartographer setting your compass on a place,
a master mending an item, and the Dark Matter Golem. The trader’s egg stands at the right of each line: “uses” (U) of
the egg lists that people’s trades, “recipes” (R) of an item shows who sells it. With **Advanced Loot Info** the viewer
also shows the mod’s creature drops and chest loot. With **Just Enough Characters** items are found by pinyin in JEI,
and the same goes for the mod’s own search fields: the journal, the storage terminal and the Tasks window.

431.content:
The machine pages are drawn like the machine's own window, and new pages show what a bioreactor eats, what grows on a Hydroponic Bed and how much oxygen it gives, and every variant of the
Flame Separator. The “+” button lays a crafting recipe out in the crafting grid of the storage terminal; a dragged item goes into its search. When the viewer shows
its item list or bookmarks, the mod's windows move aside from it and shrink only when there is no room (the “Largest” window size keeps them as they are).

432.content:
Jade shows what is inside a machine or pipe, whether it is running and which upgrades it has, whether a guardian is
asleep, who the natives are and whether they have a task for you.

433.content:
A converter links the mod’s network to the energy of other mods (Tech Reborn, AE2, Powah): on Fabric via
Team Reborn Energy, on NeoForge via the loader’s shared energy (FE). The mod’s fluids flow through other mods’ pipes and
tanks on both loaders. On NeoForge, Pipez pipes take energy straight from the mod’s generators and batteries (pipe side
set to extract) and fuel from its tanks. Buckets of the mod’s fluids empty into other mods’ tanks and fill from them
on both loaders.

434.content:
Hoppers and other mods’ item pipes put things into the input slots of the mod’s machines and take out what is ready, the same
on both loaders: modules, upgrades and rocket cargo are never pulled out by a pipe, even one that names no side, and a slot takes
no more than the machine’s window allows (16 empty canisters in the Fuel Plant’s canister slot).

435.content: The Quantum Cargo Node joins Create 6 logistics and AE2 networks of two worlds:

439.content:
With **Ponder** installed (inside Create or on its own) hold W over a machine of the mod: scenes show how to place, power, feed and empty it and why it may stand still; they are in
Ponder's index under Machines, and the node also under Create's High Logistics. On 26.3 Ponder comes with Create Fly (Fabric); on 1.21.1 and 1.20.1 it also works without Create. Both mods are optional.

440.content:
Create's zinc and other modded ores that choose biomes by the common `c:` tags generate on Thalassia on NeoForge; on both loaders the Flame Separator gives ores of other mods,
and Hemera oil burns in generators of other mods that burn lava — Tech Reborn, Thermal, Powah, Immersive Engineering, Create Crafts & Additions, Oritech.

441.content: The mod’s things are in the common `c:` tags — that is how other mods’ recipes, machines and sorters recognize them:

442.content:
ores (`c:ores`), raw materials (`c:raw_materials`), ingots (`c:ingots`), dusts (`c:dusts`), gems (`c:gems`), storage
blocks (`c:storage_blocks`), the copper sheet and gear (`c:plates`, `c:gears`);

443.content: fluid buckets (`c:buckets`), the stained glass of the worlds and other glass (`c:glass_blocks`, `c:glass_panes`);

444.content: food and drink (`c:foods` — raw and cooked meat, soups, berries; `c:drinks`), armor (`c:armors`) and weapons (`c:tools`);

445.content: world masters and lair guardians are in the entity tag `c:bosses`: other mods’ traps and teleporters leave them alone.

446.content:
Every item tag of the mod has a name in every language of the mod: a recipe viewer shows "Titanium Ingots" or "Lead Ores" instead
of `#c:ingots/titanium`. Common tags that the loader names itself (`c:ingots`, `c:ores`) keep the loader’s names.

447.content:
The mod’s crusher processes other mods’ raw materials by the same tags, and the recipes of the crusher and the zero-g
forge are ordinary data pack recipes: any pack or mod can add its own.

448.content:
With Create installed, its Crushing Wheels and Millstone process the mod’s raw ores and world stones into the same products
as the mod’s crusher, and Crushing Wheels also break down spare machine parts. On Minecraft 26.3 this is Create Fly (the Fabric
port of Create); on 1.21.1 and 1.20.1, Create itself. Without Create these recipes are simply not loaded.

449.content:
The mod works with Sodium and Iris. With a shader pack on, the mod’s post effects (climate blur, flight effects) switch
off by themselves and the telescope sky is drawn over the frame — everything else works as usual. In Sodium’s video settings the mod has
its own “Mod graphics” page (the level and a “Mod settings…” button) — on Fabric and on NeoForge.

450.content:
Tested with the Complementary Reimagined pack on Fabric and on NeoForge (Iris for NeoForge; Oculus and Embeddium have no builds
for this game version). In airless worlds and in space (the Moon, Mercury, Pluto, space, the Depths) the pack is deliberately not
applied, so the mod’s sky looks the same as without it. In other worlds the pack draws its own Earth-like sky and clouds. The pack
does not read the fog inside gas giant clouds, so the mod lays it itself: inside a cloud everything beyond seven blocks fades into the
cloud’s color, as without a pack, and the glint of cloud ore shows on top of the haze.

451.content:
The glowing parts of telescopes, machines and creatures are drawn through the shader pack's own glow program: under Iris on
Windows they no longer cause a black screen and streaks, and the game no longer crashes with Sodium's Improved Transparency.
Complementary Reimagined and Bliss are tested with this too. Post-effects can be turned on under a pack with the mod setting
Effects with shader packs, at your own risk (see Mod settings).

452.content:
Mods that change the sky (ATMOSPHERICS and the like) work on Earth and in other mods' worlds, while the mod's own worlds, space and
the telescope keep their own sky — with planets, moons, rings and nebulae. Tested with ATMOSPHERICS 2.6.8 on Forge 1.20.1.

453.content:
Mods that put a stand-in player into the world — ControlCraft cameras, machines acting as a player — work alongside the mod: it
sends nothing to a player without a real connection and leaves such a player out of its own per-player work (station orders,
landing beacon marks, progress, oxygen and climate). Carpet bots still count as players. Before 0.16.2 a ControlCraft camera
crashed the world on Forge 1.20.1 (`Exception ticking world`); NeoForge could crash the same way.

454.content: **Trinkets Updated** — accessory slots where the worlds’ artifacts and the knapsack are worn (Fabric and NeoForge).

455.content:
**Curios** (NeoForge) — the same: ring, necklace, belt, back (knapsack, the Visitor’s Sail), head (the Ringwright Lens);
with both slot mods installed, the slots of both work. You need Curios 17.0.0-beta.3 or newer: earlier betas for 26.3 do
not start on the current NeoForge. The Curios window opens with G — the same key as gear details: holding G over an
artifact opens its details, and G away from an item closes the window. Tooltips name the slot mod you have; without one
an artifact cannot be put on, and the knapsack works right from the inventory.

456.content:
**Controls on NeoForge.** NeoForge 26.3 (beta) marks many of the game’s own keys yellow — Strafe Left, Open Chat, the number
keys: they share a letter with the F3 debug combos, and the loader counts that as a conflict. The mod’s keys are not marked
there — they are judged the way the game itself and Fabric do it: gear details on G and the telescope hint on H get in the way
of neither F3+G and F3+H nor Quick Actions; a mark appears only if you rebind a key onto a taken one.

457.content: **Entity Culling** — the mod's machines, rockets on the pad, large telescopes and the shipyard are hidden behind walls like everything else (since 0.17.0).

458.content: **AsyncParticles**, **Gnetum** — work alongside: the mod's ambient effects tick on the game thread, its HUD is drawn properly in Gnetum's passes (since 0.17.0).

459.content:
**Mod Menu** — mod settings from the mod list on Fabric; on NeoForge the same button is in its own mod list, no extra
mod needed.

461.content:
**Mouse Tweaks** — works in every mod screen with slots (machine and rocket consoles, knapsacks, the dressing table, the
storage terminal, the ship and its hold, the zero-g forge): drag with the right or left button held, Shift-drag, the scroll
wheel over a slot moves items one at a time (over an output slot — the whole stack into your inventory). Over the storage list,
the ship’s hold shelf and the forge’s recipe book the wheel scrolls them, as before. The slot holding an open knapsack
stays locked for it too.

462.content:
**Carry On** — can’t pick up the mod’s rockets, shuttles and bells (cabins and parts), telescopes, the radio receiver,
the shipyard, gate hearts, airlock doors, lifts, jump beacons, battery blocks and other blocks tied to their place, nor its vehicles,
ships and masters: carrying them broke the build apart and crashed the game. Everything else (machines, chests, decor) it
carries as usual.

463.content:
**3D Skin Layers** — the knapsack and the spacesuit keep their look next to its 3D skin layers (on 26.3 before 0.16.2
bits of the knapsack showed up on the head, arms and legs).

464.content:
**Punchy! Moves** (third-person animations, with Punchy!) — the mod’s armor sets, the knapsack and the spacesuit follow the
body through its animations (before 0.16.2 the helmet and chestplate hung off the head and torso while you swung, ran or
jumped, and arms and legs poked out of the spacesuit). Punchy! alone (first person) never moved them.

465.content:
Maps (Xaero’s, JourneyMap) work in the mod’s worlds. Inventory Profiles Next leaves the mod’s own screens alone (no sort
buttons there; the storage terminal has its own); in the game’s screens it works as usual.

484.content: The Forge file is the same one on Forge 47 and on NeoForge 47.1.

485.content: Any JEI 15.x works: tested with 15.56 and 15.74.

486.content:
An addon can add its own journal nodes, worlds, constellations, events and gate conditions through the mod's Java API,
without mixins — see “Addons”.

488.content: The encyclopedia of the creatures of other worlds in the Star Journal: who lives where and who eats whom, a species card with a living model, how to study a species, a hint for stardust and the world expert.

495.content:
The **Atlas of Life** is a tab of the Star Journal that gathers the creatures of other worlds you have met: who lives in which
biome, who hunts whom and who feeds on what, how to feed, tame and breed each one and what it gives. Every player has an Atlas
of their own: on a server each one studies the creatures themselves.

496.content:
The **Atlas** tab appears in the journal header as soon as you have met any creature of another world. In a small game window
the header may have no room for it; then the Atlas opens with the **Open the Atlas of Life** button on the pages of the creature
stages: Beasts of the Worlds, Young of Another World, A Friend on Another World, In the Saddle, Life Between Worlds and others.

497.content:
On the left are the worlds where you have met someone: each has a bar of met and studied species, and a world studied in full
carries the expert's diamond. On the right is the world page or a species card.

498.content:
**Right-click a creature with the Star Journal** to open its card straight away. A species you have not met yet counts as met
right then, and its card reveals itself. The game's own creatures are not in the Atlas: for them the journal opens as usual.
Esc on such a card takes you back to the game.

499.content:
**Search** sits above the list of worlds: just start typing, or press / or Ctrl+F. The Atlas looks through the names of the
species you have met, in the game's language (pinyin works too with Just Enough Characters), and lists them in place of the
worlds; species not met yet are only counted. Enter opens the first one found, Esc clears the search.

500.content:
**Who lives where**: a line for every biome of the world and the creatures that live in it. Species that live not in a biome
but in ruins, come with events or fly under the open sky get their own line, Ruins, events and the open sky. Creatures you have
not met yet show as a "?": the Atlas does not tell for free where they live.

501.content:
**Food chains**: predators on top, their prey below, and the food of the world (its plants and fare) at the bottom. Threads run
from the eater to its food, red for the hunt and green for eating, with sparks running along them. A thread shows once the
eater is studied.

502.content: **Masters and guardians**: at the bottom of the page, the master of the world and the guardians of its lairs.

503.content:
The card holds a living model of the creature: drag to turn it, use the wheel to zoom. The model plays its moves by itself
(rest, move, strike, graze, sleep, dance) until you pick one; its looks are adult, young, shorn and harnessed, where the species
has them. On the right are the study steps, the **Next step** (what to do next) and the sections that open step by step:

504.content:
| Step | How to earn it                                      | What it opens                                          |
| ---- | --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Met  | come within sight of the creature (up to 24 blocks) | where it lives; danger: health, blow, armor, abilities |

505.content:
| Step    | How to earn it                                                                              | What it opens                       |
| ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Studied | stay near it for half a minute (up to 16 blocks, in sight) while it goes about its business | notes, habits, keeping; +1 stardust |

506.content:
| Step   | How to earn it                                                                                     | What it opens                        |
| ------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Sample | get a part of it by shears, brush or pickaxe where it allows, trade for one or take it by the hunt | what it drops and where its parts go |

507.content:
| Step        | How to earn it                                                          | What it opens |
| ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------- |
| Tamed, Bred | for species that can be tamed and give young, as in the Husbandry guide | —             |

508.content: A **spyglass** studies from afar and twice as fast: look at the creature through it, up to 64 blocks away.

567.content:
A pair of  joins the storages of two worlds. In the storage terminal of one you see the things of the other, send
things there and take them from there — even while the far end is not loaded.

568.content:
Put a node against a terminal or cell on each world, give both energy and click one and then the other with the tuning fork: a double helix rises
over each. Only the owner and their team see and take the far end's things.

573.content: One thing costs 1 ⚡ of the pair's store of 256,000 ⚡, which the energy of both nodes fills.

574.content:
**Sending**: put things into the node's send slots by hand, hopper or pipe. They leave for the far end at once and unload when that place is
loaded; if there is no storage against the far node, they lie in its tray.

575.content:
**The list**: things of the far end are marked in the terminal; the tooltip tells how many are here and how many there, on which world, and how
old the list is. “All / Here / There” filter the list.

576.content:
**Taking** wakes the far end for a minute: click a thing, and a couple of seconds later click again. Waking costs 8 ⚡ a second for each chunk of
the zone and needs five seconds' worth in the store at once; at most four far ends are awake.

577.content: A server owner can turn waking off with the `cargo_wake` game rule — then only sending works.

578.content:
**Create**: a Stock Link right against the node sees the far network; the Stock Keeper orders from another world, own stock first. Works with Create
Fly on 26.3 Fabric, with Create on 1.21.1 NeoForge and on 1.20.1. With Ponder installed hold W over the node.

579.content:
**AE2**: a cable right against the node (a channel and 1 AE a tick): the ME terminal shows the far network's things, your own go first, what does
not fit goes to the other world. Works on 26.3 and 1.21.1 NeoForge and on 1.20.1. There is no crafting by the far network.

607.content:
The Dark Matter Golem is an iron block between two lightning rods, woken by a grain of dark
matter. It hangs where it was made, bubbles of its matter circle it, and sparks leap from its copper points. The golem does not
fight: it **trades the goods of one road for those of another**, one for two.

608.content: Put a lightning rod on an iron block and another one under it (weathered ones work too).

609.content: Click the iron block with ; they come from the dark matter cloud of the Main Belt.

610.content:
The scene fades to violet, two bolts of lightning strike the upper point, a glowing pattern spreads seven blocks over the ground,
and the golem turns to the one who built it. The grain is spent (not in creative mode). The first build is the Star Journal
stage Dark Matter Golem (after Sky Anomalies); the stage has a blueprint in the journal.

611.content:
The golem can stand anywhere: on Earth, at your base, on your own station. It drifts back to where it was built if moved, and
turns to the nearest player. Only a player can hurt it; broken, it gives back the iron block and the two lightning rods.

630.content:
Every big dungeon has a mechanism of its own, on every level. Wait by the door for one turn: see where it warns, what it does and for how long — then
go, it repeats. A mechanism runs only while someone is near, is the same for all players and goes back when everyone leaves; a grate or shutter waits

650.content: Step by step: Dungeons: what each one is about.

652.content: Where to find the floor key in every dungeon: what the gate socket tells you, how to spot loose stones and where the Gatekeeper’s Eye lies.

653.content: The gate socket tells you where the key is

657.content: The key is gone, or the dungeon is old

659.content:
A world’s dungeon has several floors, and from each one a **gate** leads down. Some gates are held by a puzzle (mirrors,
rune plates) or by the floor’s guardian, others by a **keystone socket**: it waits for a key, and until it gets one you
cannot go further. The key **never has to be crafted**: it lies on the same floor, in its own room, and that room can be
reached from the floor’s entrance without opening the gate.

660.content: Press the socket with an empty hand (or with anything that is not the key). Two lines appear under the crosshair:

661.content:
the first says which key the socket wants: “The socket awaits its key: …” (Jade and WTHIT show the same line when you
look at the socket);

662.content:
the second, in **teal**, says in which room of this floor the key lies and how it is hidden, for example: “The key is on
this floor, in the gatekeeper’s room: behind loose stones under the eye carved in the wall…”.

663.content:
The socket does not tell you the way to the room. The room’s name says what is in it (a store, a locker, a cell, a workshop,
someone’s lodgings) — look for a room furnished like that on the floor; the floor’s notes on lecterns often hint at who keeps
the key. Once you have the key, press the socket with it: the key goes into the socket, and the
gate down opens.

664.content:
Most often the key is walled up behind **loose stones**. You can tell them from four or five steps away if you know what to
look for:

665.content: the mortar has crumbled out of **every joint**, the joints are dark, the stones sit askew, and a crack runs through them;

666.content: sparks flicker in the joints, and a **draft** blows from the gaps — dust drifts out of every open side;

667.content: now and then grit trickles quietly out of the gaps — you can hear it;

668.content:
in Jade and WTHIT the stones are named like ordinary masonry, but under the name stands “The stones shift: they will give
to a hand”.

669.content:
How to open them: **right-click them** — with an empty hand or with something in it (just not while sneaking with an item).
The stones crumble, and behind them is a niche with a chest. No pickaxe is needed, and it works **in Adventure mode** too.
The Mining Fatigue that weighs on you while the dungeon’s master lives does not get in the way of loose stones.

670.content:
Not every patch of loose stones hides a key: caches of supplies are walled up the same way (the room’s note speaks of them),
and so are secret passages into neighboring rooms. The key is behind the one the socket told you about.

671.content:
The table is built from the mod’s data — the same data the gate sockets write their hint from. The floor is counted from the
top (1 is the uppermost). A floor missing from the table has a gate held by a puzzle or a guardian, not by a key.

672.content:
“A thing of the world” is a key that was not made for the dungeon but is found in the world (a core, a gland, a feather,
a plate): the socket takes any such item, not only the one that lay in the key room. The dungeons’ own keys (the eye, the
core, the seals, the hailstone and the rest) lie in the key rooms.

673.content:
is the key to the gate of the **fourth floor** of the Selenite Catacombs on the Moon, the Necropolis level. Without
it the gate of the necropolis, behind which the Moon’s master sleeps, does not open. You do not craft the eye: it is walled
up in the wall of the **gatekeeper’s room** on that same fourth floor.

675.content: Go down to floor 4 and press the socket of the necropolis gate — the teal line names the gatekeeper’s room.

676.content:
Walk the floor: the gatekeeper’s room is a small room you can reach from the stairs from floor 3 without opening the gate.
Inside there is a stone chair facing the wall, a bed in the corner, a table with a lectern and the sarcophagus the
gatekeeper prepared for himself. A hunter guards the room.

677.content:
On the wall in front of the chair an **eye is carved**, its pupil glowing. Right under it are loose stones: crumbled joints,
sparks, a draft. The gatekeeper’s note on the lectern says the same: the eye is walled in “beneath its own sign, behind
stones that will give to a hand”.

678.content: Press the stones under the eye with your hand — they crumble, and in the niche behind them is a chest with the eye.

679.content: Go back to the socket and set the eye in: the gate to the master opens.

680.content: The room may have other loose stones too — a secret passage into the next room. The eye is under the sign of the eye.

681.content:
**A dungeon from an older version of the mod.** The socket’s hint works in dungeons placed before it too: the socket in the
world remembers its group, and the text comes from the translation. Press the socket — the teal line will appear.

682.content:
**The chest is empty.** The key room’s chest gives one key, and in multiplayer whoever opens it first takes it. Ask your
companions: maybe they already have the key, or the gate is already open.

683.content:
**The key is lost.** A world has more than one dungeon. The same world’s key from another dungeon fits this socket: the
socket checks which item is set in, not which chest it came from. A key that is a thing of the world can simply be gathered again.

684.content:
**There is no room by that name on the floor.** In dungeons of newer versions the key room always stands; if it is missing
in a dungeon placed by an older version, take the key from another dungeon of the same world.

685.content: The rest about dungeons — puzzles, ambushes, Mining Fatigue, the master’s arena: “Dungeons and world masters”.

688.content: The worlds’ dungeons, puzzles, the master’s altar and what bosses give.

691.content:
Every world has a **dungeon** — an underground of many different rooms on several levels: puzzles, traps, guardians and
treasuries. At its heart stands the **altar of the world’s master**.

692.content: A map to the dungeon comes from the world’s inhabitants and from finds in its structures.

693.content: The dungeon’s puzzles are blocks to press, turn or set in the right order; dungeon keys open the doors.

694.content:
**Floor keys.** The gate down from a floor waits for a key of that dungeon (on the Moon, floor 4 wants the Gatekeeper’s Eye).
Click the gate socket without the key, and it tells you in which room of this floor the key lies and how it is hidden —
most often behind **loose stones**: masonry with dark crumbled seams and a crack, with sparks in the joints and a draft of
dust from the gaps (sometimes you hear grit trickling). Press it with your hand (right click, also in Adventure) — it
crumbles, and the key chest is behind it. The key never has to be crafted, and the key room is always on its floor,
before the gate. Where every dungeon’s key lies and how to find the Gatekeeper’s Eye —
“Dungeon keys”.

695.content:
An offering on the altar **summons the master**: what and how much to place is on the boss page and in the recipe
viewer.

696.content:
While the master lives, **the masonry holds**: inside the dungeon you get Mining Fatigue V, and the best pickaxe takes
about a minute per block of masonry — there is no digging past the master to the treasury. After the victory it lifts.

697.content:
**Ambush** — a room with a signal plate: step in and bars close the doorways, and creatures rise from the floor wave after
wave. Leave in the middle of the fight (walk out, die) and the bars crumble after fifteen seconds, but the ambush remembers
the waves you beat: when you come back, you meet the wave you left at. An ambush never leaves you locked in with something
you cannot reach: a creature that hangs under the vault or slips behind the bars and stays out of the fight for a quarter
of a minute sinks into the floor and comes up again next to you.

762.content: Capital ships of your own: how to get one, what is aboard, how to call and move it, crew and boundaries.

767.content:
A freighter is a capital ship 150 to 950 blocks long that carries your base through space: a hangar for your ships, a hold of
storage cells, a hall to build in, crew rooms and a bridge. It stays in open space — the Solar System, the Interrift, the Depths,
the far roads — and never lands in a world. One freighter per player.

772.content:
Every hull is put together from its own bow, middle, stern, citadel and mast and painted in one of six faction palettes: the
bridge window and the station market show the parts by name.

773.content:
**A distress call.** Fly an armed ship in open space, away from stations, for about ten minutes: the instruments catch a call.
Come closer than 220 blocks and shoot down the Drifters — those at the breaches first; the bar at the top is the freighter's hull.
Then answer the captain (;) and take the ship. The first call is always class C; later ones come after an hour of flight
and may be of any class. Everyone who dealt 20 damage gets an offer of their own, and it waits three game days.

774.content: **A station.** The order board of every people's station has “Freighters & Frigates”: three ships a day, with a drawing you can turn.

| ----- | -------------------------------- | ------------ |

779.content: Trust makes it cheaper. Payment comes from your inventory and from the hold of the ship on the pad.

780.content:
**An exchange.** A freighter you already own counts for half the price of its class. The base stays exactly where it stands, the hold
and the ships move over, the key is the same. If something does not fit, the list says what and how much — and nothing is taken.

781.content: A lost key is replaced for 4 of the station's supply at any board that sells freighters.

782.content:
In open space use the , or the “Call the Freighter” key (unbound by default; the key item may lie
anywhere in the inventory), or the button in your ship's console: the freighter jumps in with its hangar toward you. It is free.

783.content: Fly into the glowing hangar mouth on the port side and you step out on the deck. You may also fly in on foot in a spacesuit.

784.content: Leave by ship through the hangar console (sneak-click picks the next ship), on foot through the airlock, in a spacesuit.

785.content: The command console on the bridge moves the freighter itself — to a body of the system or to your ship.

786.content:
The floor lines lead the way: amber to the hangar, white to the tower. Stand in an antigrav shaft and hold jump or sneak to ride up
and down; the chart table on the command deck opens the map of the decks. There is air and Earth's gravity. Walls cannot be broken,
you build in the hall, and machines work there as anywhere while somebody is on the decks. The bunks set no spawn point.

787.content:
**The boundary.** An invisible boundary stands behind the walls and windows: creative flight, elytra, pearls, chorus fruit, boats,
explosions, broken windows and other mods' teleports stay inside. The ways out are the hangar, the pilot seat, the hatch and the airlock
(an operator's `/tp` works). Ship decks and raid decks have the same boundary.

788.content:
**Friends.** The bridge console keeps the freighter's own list: friends dock, walk and build; calling and jumping is for the owner,
and a ship leaves the hangar only with someone who may fly it.

789.content: Frigates, expeditions and the dreadnought: “Fleet and dreadnought”.

793.content: Gate rings on every world: how to awaken them and travel between worlds without transport.

795.content:
Every world, Earth included, has a **gate ring** — a nine-by-nine square without corners, standing on its edge: 27 frames
and a heart at the bottom. It is a road between worlds that bypasses rockets — but only between gates you have awakened.

796.content: While the **master of the world** lives, that world’s gate sleeps. Defeat it and a heart remains that awakens the gate.

797.content:
Gate blocks cannot be destroyed: neither the Wither, nor the dragon, nor pistons can take them. An unfinished ring can
be taken apart while sneaking, with an empty hand.

798.content: The ring takes the color of the world it stands in.

799.content: Every passage has a fee — the recipe viewer and the tooltip at the gate show it.

800.content: On Earth, in the End and in the Nether the gates ask for something of their own — the journal will tell you.

801.content: The heart for a gate comes from the master of the world: “Dungeons and world masters”.

802.content: Who set the rings and what they left behind — “Watch Rings and the Lens”.

804.content: The Nether's own trade: Giant remains, layered magma under pressure, the heat probe, the digger's chisel, the coolant lance, the Giant's cradle and the everlasting hearth.

809.content: What to do with the bones

812.content:
The Giants once walked the fire road, and their bones still lie in the rock of the Nether — centuries in magma have fired them
like clay. Once a vent is open (stage 1, see “Nether and End changes”), the remains come alive:
the rock around the fired bones is shot through with **layered magma under pressure**. You dig carefully here: open a pocket
the wrong way and you get lava in your face and cracked bones. While the Nether sleeps or the changes are switched off, the rock
at the remains is cold: neither bone nor magma can be broken — "The bone is held fast by cold rock: while the Nether sleeps, it will not come out."

813.content:
A **Giant Remains** is a mound of rock under arches of broken ribs; a skull peeks out of the slope, and four more bones lie one or
two blocks under the face. Remains lie in soul sand valleys, basalt deltas and nether wastes (not in the forests). A vent breach
sometimes blows remains out of the slope next to the new mouth — so remains come to old worlds too.

814.content: Five Giants, each with their own skull and their own mound rock:

820.content:
Bones give themselves away: during the Blue Draft a blue light flickers in the slopes, and a bonedigger
scratches the ground right above a bone.

821.content:
has a pressure from 0 to 3. A pocket is a set of connected magma blocks (up to 32). It answers
when an empty space appears next to it (air, fire, grass; rock, lava and water do not count):

822.content:
| Pressure | What happens when it is opened                                                |
| -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1–2      | the pocket **vents** steam — the pressure of the whole pocket drops by a step |

823.content:

| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 3        | the pocket **swells** white-hot, hisses and spurts (everyone within 8 blocks is warned); a second and a half — plug the hole, pour coolant or run |

824.content:
| Pressure    | What happens when it is opened                                                                                                                             |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 3, too late | **a blowout**: lava into the opened cells, fire, 5 damage and knockback to everyone within 4 blocks, bones nearby crack; after 5 seconds the lava goes out |

825.content:
Breaking a full pocket itself blows it out at once. Every hidden bone has a chain 3 → 2 → 1 toward the nearest face: dig from
that side, and each venting turns a two into a one and a three into a two. Under the skull lies a three, under the middle of the
mound a sealed pocket of threes: only coolant takes it.

826.content:
The  in hand shows the magma within 4 blocks behind the face you look at as glowing spots: dark
cherry — 1, orange — 2, trembling whitish yellow — 3, gray-blue — cooled; bones are cold blue spots. Use it on rock for
a reading: how many pockets are near, the fullest one, how many bones.

827.content:
The  — **only with it** does a bone come out whole (or cracked, if it already cracked); any other
tool crumbles it into 1–3 . Take a bone out next to a full three and it comes out cracked, and
the pocket blows.

828.content: A  on an opened pocket cools the whole pocket to zero (the empty canister comes back).

829.content:
The  is set point first into the rock and once a second cools the pocket up to three blocks behind
by a step, **without opening** it. Coolant comes through fuel pipes or from a canister (tank 4000, a canister adds 1000).

830.content:
The  is the headstone; 3 by 5  are laid in front of it. Bones are put
as items on the stones of the middle row, each in its own place, from the headstone: skull, ,
, , . A bone in the wrong place —
a line tells you whose place it is.

831.content:
The cradle can face any of the four sides: it runs away from the headstone the way you look when you place it. Cradle stones
turn by themselves so that their gold-lined groove runs along the cradle — whichever way you look when you place them, and even if
you lay them before the headstone; a stone away from a cradle lies the way you look. The Giant lies on its back: the skull looks
up at the sky with its crown toward the headstone, and the hand at the far end spreads its fingers outward.

832.content:
A whole skeleton of one Giant brings the strong moment **The Giant Remembers**: light in the Giant's color, veins across the floor
with the vent sign, a shadow of heat over the cradle and a line of the Giant's memory over the uplink. A few seconds later the
cradle becomes an **everlasting hearth**:

833.content:
a  by the headstone (beside it, above it or two blocks above) burns without fuel and never
cools down;

834.content:
within 12 blocks of the cradle **the cold of the world does not reach you** — of any world (heat stays): a cradle works in the
Ash and on the ice giants alike;

835.content: every 5 seconds the players in its warmth get **the Giant's gift**:

| Forge-Smith | mends the things in your hands and those you wear |

841.content: Take the cradle apart and the hearth goes out, the bones come off; build it again and the Giant remembers again.

842.content:
Whole bones make gear of the fire road: the  (fire and lava −35%, an absorption shield every
30 seconds) and the  (strikes whoever hits you with heat and knocks them back, every 2 seconds).

843.content:
Cracked ones () and chips make ,
