844.content:
In the Vents chapter, after Vent Mouth: Giant Remains, Heat Probe, Digger's Chisel, Ease the Pressure (open a pocket at
pressure 1 or 2 or cool it with coolant), Fired Bone (take a bone out whole with the chisel), Giant's Cradle, The Giant Remembers
(a whole skeleton of one Giant) and Five Giants (the memory of all five).

845.content: What else changes in the Nether and the End — “Nether and End changes”.

847.content: At the bottom of the vents lie the fire worlds, and the bell goes down there: “Magmascope”.

849.content: How to feed creatures of other worlds by hand, breed them and raise their young; herds sleeping together and dancing by a jukebox; shearing and gathering from the living, herds with a leader, predators and prey; taming and mounts.

860.content:
Some peaceful creatures of other worlds eat from your hand, have young and keep their own routine: by day they graze and
sniff around, at night the whole herd lies down to sleep. They take **only the food of their own world** — you will not
breed a Martian roller on Earth wheat. The first three kinds: the Canyon Roller
of Mars, the Moon Hopper and the Mist Lamb of the Breath.

861.content:
| Creature      | World | Food | Grazes by          |
| ------------- | ----- | ---- | ------------------ |
| Canyon Roller | Mars  |      | Hematite Blueberry |

862.content:
| Creature    | World | Food | Grazes by       |
| ----------- | ----- | ---- | --------------- |
| Moon Hopper | Moon  |      | Earthshine Lily |

863.content:
| Creature  | World  | Food | Grazes by      |
| --------- | ------ | ---- | -------------- |
| Mist Lamb | Breath |      | Sourberry Bush |

864.content:
A creature notices the food in your hand from a dozen blocks away: it sniffs, then trots after you and stops a couple of
steps short. Click it with the food and it eats from your hand: a hurt one heals, a baby grows faster (each feeding takes
a tenth off its time), and a grown one **falls in love** — hearts float up above it. If there is nothing the food would do
(healthy and already in love), you keep it.

865.content:
Two of a kind in love find each other and, after a few seconds side by side, have a **baby** — with a wreath of hearts and
a little experience for whoever fed them. The first young completes the journal stage “Young of Another World”. After
having young the parents rest for five minutes. Bred creatures and their parents stay by the farm: they do not wander off
or vanish while you are away.

866.content:
**Only in their own world.** On Earth or any other strange world a creature eats but turns away: dim little stars fade
above it — the wrong sky — and the line above the hotbar says it is in no mood for young here.

867.content: **Not when crowded.** With twelve or more of its kind around, food only heals: “Too crowded”.

868.content:
A baby is half the size of a grown one, big-headed and paler; it keeps close to the nearest grown one of its kind and grows
up in twenty minutes — faster if you feed it. When it grows up, it sparkles with gold.

869.content:
As in the base game, a spawn egg used on a grown creature of the same kind gives a baby beside it (the egg is used up outside
Creative mode). This works only for kinds that have babies; on the others the egg does nothing.

870.content:
With nothing to do, a creature grazes by a plant of its world (it never eats the plant itself), sniffs, looks around. At
night the herd lies down almost at once: the roller curls into a ball, the hopper folds its dish ears, the lamb tucks in its
legs and the mist of its fleece settles. “z”s drift up from the sleepers. Dawn wakes them, and so does a blow, food in your
hand or a player running past — walk. Flyers with folding wings (the ion vulture, the bolt petrel, the ember swift) land
to rest on the ground, a ledge or a cloud top, and sleep only while perched; come close and they take off. By a playing jukebox and next to a working radio telescope, creatures dance: the
roller bounces and rolls over as a ball, the hopper hops on the spot, the lamb sways in the air.

871.content:
Some creatures grow back what you take from them — no need to kill them. Click the creature with the right tool: what you take
scatters next to it, the creature shakes itself, and a line above the hotbar tells you how long the regrowth takes. Until it
grows back there is nothing to take; its regrowth food makes it grow back at once. Babies are not sheared, and a tamed creature
only by its owner.

878.content:
A sheared lamb is a smooth lilac barrel without its puffs of mist; the crab keeps stumps of the chipped spires on its hump; the
grub's cap has no drips. Cloud Wool goes into Cloud Felt and the armor of the Breath. Shears, brushes and pickaxes of other mods work too. A chipped sparsaur keeps only stumps of its ridge, a brushed skink a stubby tail, and a glassneck's tear drops go dark.

879.content:
Sclera Grazers of the Eye and Bone Gnawers of the Ash
move as a herd: one leader wanders, the rest keep a ring around it and catch up when they fall behind. The leader is the one who
came first; if it dies, another leads. A straggler finds the nearest herd within a couple of seconds.

880.content:
A hungry predator looks out for prey of its own world: the Ring Shark of Saturn hunts Ring
Gliders, Bone Gnawers hunt Ember Mice. As it gives chase it raises the alarm — all the prey nearby scatters. Caught prey is
eaten and leaves nothing behind, and a fed predator leaves everyone alone for a few minutes. Predators never touch your tamed
or bred creatures, nor babies near you.

881.content:
Three creatures of other worlds can be tamed: the sclera grazer of the Eye with a
crystalline lens (), the storm ray of Jupiter with a float
bladder (), and the under-ice whale of Europa with its
own lumen (). Feed it from your hand again and again: now and then it trusts you a little more —
a heart floats up; a gray wisp means "not yet". Trust grows only toward the one who feeds: food from another hand, or a
blow, starts it over. Once it trusts you fully, a golden ring spreads around it and it is yours (journal stage "A Friend on
Another World").

882.content:
**Empty hand** — "sit" or "follow". A tamed creature follows you, catches up when it falls behind, and appears beside you
if you have gone far.

883.content: **When you are away** (logged out, on another world) it waits at home, where you were last together.

884.content: **Release** — sneak and click with an empty hand while holding its food in the other hand: it is wild again but stays.

885.content:
**Someone else's** tamed creature can be fed (food heals it), but not commanded, saddled or sheared: "not yours, its owner
is …". It can only be hurt if the server allows players to fight.

886.content:
Each of the three takes a **harness made from its own world**:  for the grazer,
 for the ray,  for the whale. Click your tamed creature with the
harness and a saddle and straps appear on it; an empty hand gets you into the saddle; sneaking with an empty hand tells it to sit or follow; shears take the
harness off.

887.content:
| Mount         | Moves                       | Notes                                                                             |
| ------------- | --------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| sclera grazer | on land, at a trot or a run | jump key — a jump to Earth height in any gravity; no harm from falls of two jumps |

888.content:
| Mount     | Moves                | Notes                                                                  |
| --------- | -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| storm ray | flies where you look | jump key — up; hangs still without input; out of stamina — glides down |

889.content:
| Mount           | Moves                | Notes                                                                               |
| --------------- | -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| under-ice whale | swims where you look | never leaves the water; you stay in the saddle underwater and breathe your own suit |

890.content:
**A gait of its own under the saddle.** The grazer trots, and when you sprint it breaks into a gallop — neck stretched,
tail flying — and tucks its forelegs when it jumps; the ray beats its wings hard when climbing or dashing, glides in level
flight and sweeps its wings back in a dive; the whale swims in long waves and drives with its tail on a dash. Mounts lean
into turns, tip their nose along the way and turn their head where you look.

891.content:
**Stamina.** Running (the sprint key) and climbing spend the mount's stamina — its bar appears above your hearts; walking and
rest bring it back, food from your hand restores it at once. Out of stamina, no running. On the run, wind lines streak along the
edges of the screen, dust flies from the grazer's feet, lightning from the ray's wings, and a glowing trail follows the whale.

892.content:
A mount **never leaves its world**: with a rider it will not go through a portal, and gates, rifts and the mod's transport set the rider down. Wherever a mount already stands (say, placed with a spawn egg on Earth), you can ride it there. Two hundred blocks in the saddle complete the
journal stage "In the Saddle". Log out in the saddle and the mount leaves with you and comes back when you return.

948.content: How to breathe in airless worlds and endure heat, cold and acid.

950.content: Open space: walking in zero gravity

955.content:
You cannot breathe in the mod’s worlds. There is air in a dome, in a sealed room, in a rocket cabin — and in the space
suit, while its tank holds oxygen.

956.content:
The suit protects only **when worn complete**: , ,
, . It is not armor but a layer of its own: you put it
on and take it off at the , and armor is worn over it.

957.content:
The chestplate holds the oxygen, the charge and the modules: four module slots — tanks, regenerator, cooling unit, heating unit,
power cell, solar film. Modules are fitted at the , which also refills the chestplate
with oxygen and charge.

958.content:
A new chestplate is **empty**: before you fly, open an  or a suit rack while wearing the
suit, and it fills it. If there is nothing to breathe and the tank is empty or the suit is not complete, a line lights up
above the hotbar: what happened and where to take shelter — in the rocket cabin or under a dome.

959.content:
Outside a ship in the void there is almost no weight. Three chestplate modules are made for going outside — they take the
same four slots as air and warmth, so you have to choose:

960.content:
— the MMU pack: you fly where you look; jump is up, sneak is down, and with no keys it holds you
in place. It uses the chestplate’s charge: an empty pack does not pull.

961.content:
— magnetic boots: hold you on metal (iron, station plating and decks, the mod’s metals)
and on the hull of a ship or a drifting rock (the Visitor, belt rocks). Standing on a flying ship, you ride with it.
A comet nucleus does not hold: it tumbles.

962.content:
— the safety tether hooks to the ship you stepped out of. Drift farther than 32 blocks and it
pulls you back; beyond 96 blocks or without the ship it snaps.

963.content: — stores oxygen and refills suits, even while worn.

964.content:
The bioreactor — kelp, leaves, crops and plants of other worlds make oxygen; it needs energy. The electrolyzer makes it of water or rock:
“Air for a base”.

965.content: The pump fills a **sealed room**; a dome holds a sphere of air even without walls.

966.content: Oxygen flows through pipes: every installation is a node of the network with its own store.

967.content:
Fire needs oxygen just like you do. Where there is nothing to breathe, torches, lanterns, candles, campfires and fire go out half
a second after they are placed: a puff of soot, dying embers and a hiss. Flint and steel only sparks in a vacuum.

968.content:
In a **sealed room**, under an **oxygen dome** and in station halls fire burns. When a room loses its air (an open airlock,
a broken wall) its flames go out within a few seconds, together with the air.

969.content:
A torch or a lantern becomes **snuffed**: no light, and it breaks into the original torch or lantern. It does not relight by
itself — use flint and steel where there is air. Candles and campfires simply go out.

970.content: What to light the way with outside: glowstone, sea lanterns, station lamps, the lanterns of world sets — they are not fire.

971.content: What goes out is set by the block tag `burns_oxygen`: a modpack can add its own torches to it.

972.content:
Worlds can be hot or cold, and Venus has acid. Overheating and freezing build up gradually: the screen shimmers with
haze or frosts over, and your movements slow down. Suit modules, shelters and the worlds’ food protect you; against acid —
the acid-proof coating of the chestplate and an  near the base. Deep inside a large dungeon
the world’s acid does not reach you at all, and heat and cold are much weaker; by a window or under an open shaft it is as outside. When the gauge reaches a quarter, a line
above the hotbar says what will save you, and the journal names what the suit needs in each world in the landing task:

1095.content: Which face takes what, pushing output, copying a setup, switching a machine off with redstone and energy between touching machines.

1100.content: Every machine of the mod can be told which of its six faces takes and gives what — as in Mekanism — and any redstone signal switches it off.

1101.content:
Open the machine's window and press **Sides**. Choose what you set up — input, canisters, fuel, output, upgrades, fluid or energy; only
what this machine has is shown — and click the faces on the model: **none → input → output → both**, the other mouse button goes back. Faces are
counted from the machine's front.

1102.content:
**By default** items go in from above and from the sides, output comes out below, fluid and energy pass through every face. Upgrade cards are
closed to hoppers until you open them.

1103.content: **Pushing output** (off by default): once a second the machine puts what is ready into the chest or machine beyond an output face.

1104.content: **Copy setup** and **Paste setup** move it to another machine. The setup stays in the machine's item when you break it.

1105.content: It works with hoppers, the mod's pipes and pneumatic mail, and other mods' pipes on every loader.

1106.content:
The fuel plant takes canisters from a hopper above; the fuel depot takes canisters from hoppers and pipes (full ones to drain, empty ones to
fill) and gives them out below. The electric furnace takes only what can be smelted.

1107.content:
A lever, button, wire or comparator stops a machine: no work, no energy, fuel or air used, no sound or particles. A sign hovers over it, and the
window and Jade say “Switched off by a redstone signal”. A lift finishes its ride and a drone its flight first. The same Sides page makes a machine
deaf to redstone.

1108.content:
Machines standing face to face share energy **without a beam**: an output face against an input face, or batteries evening out with each other.
Consumers come first, what is left goes into batteries. A face closed to energy stops it, redstone stops it; a consumer does not pass energy on,
a battery does. Beams of the grid do not look at sides. In old worlds machines already standing side by side start sharing, because energy is
open on all faces by default.

1112.content: Machine tiers, the resonance energy network, pipes and base logistics.

1117.content:
Every machine has four tiers — **Mk1–Mk4**: the higher the tier, the more power and upgrade slots. Numbers and all tiers
are in the machine reference.

1118.content:
Energy travels through the **resonance network** — beams of light between the machines’ lenses. The first source is the
; by day under the open sky a solar panel works, and a battery stores the surplus
(2×2×2 and 3×3×3 cubes grow together into a big battery). The induction emitter powers machines inside its field without
beams, losing a quarter. The energy converter links the network to the energy of other mods.

1119.content:
**Storage keeps its contents.** A broken battery block (and a battery assembled from blocks: the broken part takes its share), oxygen tank,
fuel depot, launch gantry, pearl liquefier, cryo still, bioreactor, generator or fuel plant drops as an item with its charge, fluid and
installed upgrade cards; the item's tooltip and bar show the reserve. This also holds for explosions and for blocks broken by
other mods, and neither the contents nor the cards are duplicated. **Upgrading keeps it too:** the next tier of any machine or storage
cell is crafted from the previous tier and that tier's machine core, and the charge, fluid, cards, stored items and name move into
the new item.

1120.content:
**Machine windows work like any container.** Shift-click moves a stack between a machine's slots and your inventory: an item
goes to a slot that takes it, and if none does, the window says why. Shift-double-click moves every stack of that item from the same
side at once.

1121.content:
**Touching machines need no beam.** Machines standing face to face share energy by the settings of their sides — see
“Machine sides and redstone”, which also tells which face takes what and how redstone switches a machine off.

1122.content:
**The window of a machine** is a live drawing of the machine itself: what is inside is painted into it, a line runs from the input through the machine to the output, the color of the
nameplate tells working, stopped or switched off, and a stopped machine names the reason — a full tray, an item without a recipe, missing parts, too little energy. Clicking the line
opens the recipes in JEI or REI. Graphics settings can lighten it.

1123.content: With Ponder installed hold W over a machine to see how to place, power and feed it. And every machine has a page of the Manual.

1124.content: Fuel, coolant and oxygen flow through pipes. The mod’s fluids work with other mods’ pipes and tanks.

the  fills a , the  —
a  (empty canisters go into the slot on the right; without them the liquid goes into the pipes).
The  turns any fuel into canisters and back. It holds one fuel: an empty one is switched with the button
in its panel or takes whatever is poured into it (a bucket, a canister, a pipe of another mod). Take the fuel out with an empty bucket or

The fuel plant spoils nothing when you change its raw material: the old fuel stays in its tank until it leaves by pipe, bucket or

with a click or put into its window; a bucket of that fuel works too.

1159.content: How to find a fallen meteorite by its column of smoke, its glow or its white beam, and what to take from the crater.

1167.content:
Once every few days a  falls to the Earth. It falls **away from dwellings** — only on wild land,
with no buildings, beds or villager workstations; there is no explosion, and it leaves no fire. On the Moon a meteorite falls
during its event — the **meteor shower**: shooting stars stream across the black sky from one point, small stones strike
the regolith around you (each leaves a pit with a dark stone and  under it), and at the height
of the shower one great meteorite comes down with its crater and white beam.

1168.content:
The meteor comes in from the player's side and draws a streak across the whole sky: by day — fire with a smoky tail,
by night — a white-hot column and the cross-shaped glint of its head. The impact is a flash, a pillar of fire for a moment,
a shock wave, a shake and a spray of embers. The chat names the direction: “A meteorite has fallen to the north. Look for
the column of smoke, and at night for the glow”.

1169.content:
Meteorites do not litter the area around your base: they fall 80–120 blocks from a player, but never within 192 blocks of
a player's bed or respawn anchor or the world spawn, and never within 128 blocks of a recent crater. A player who never leaves
home waits in vain: the meteorite waits until someone heads out into the wilds.

1170.content:
Over a fresh crater a sign stands for **ten minutes** — or until its core is mined. It is seen from afar, beyond the render
distance, by day and by night:

half minute it fades out. Once the core is mined, the sign goes out at once. Up close, glowing cracks run across the ground

1274.content: Stages of the End and the Nether: Sewn Seams and Split Seams, vent mouths, new weather and events, the creatures of the End and the Nether themselves, and the server owner's switch.

1286.content: Creatures of the End and the Nether

1288.content:
The Nether and the End are no longer just platforms for instruments and transport: they **change as you play**. An opened
rift or vent, a slain guardian and a flight beyond it raise the world's **stage** — the seams on the End islands come apart,
the vent mouths of the Nether heat up, and their own weather, events and creatures arrive. The instrument sky and the journal
are personal, but the changes themselves are shared by the whole server.

1289.content:
A stage belongs to the End and to the Nether themselves, not to a player: the **first** one to open what is needed raises it,
and everyone sees the changes. A stage only goes up.

1296.content:
**Old worlds** catch up: when a player enters the End or the Nether, the world learns what they have opened before (rifts,
vents, flights, the dragon, Withers killed) — and the stage takes its place.

1297.content:
The most visible changes follow not the whole world but the **place**: in the End, the side of the sky of an open rift;
in the Nether, the biomes of an open vent (below).

1298.content:
The changes can be switched off: the game rule **Nether and End changes** (in the Game Rules screen or with `/gamerule`;
on 26.3 it is `<mod id>:nether_end_changes`, on 1.21.1 and 1.20.1 `<mod id>.nether_end_changes`) or the line
`"nether_end_changes": false` in `config/<mod id>-server.json` (read when the server starts). The changes run only when
both are on.

1299.content:
Switched off, stages and opened places still build up, but the world does not show them: seams fall asleep, vent mouths
cool down, stage weather and events do not come, new creatures do not come out, the Void Shoals and the Giant digs stand
still. Switch it back on and everything returns within a second. An operator reads and sets the stage with the mod's
command `stage end|nether [get|set N]`.

1373.content: The worlds’ inhabitants: trading, talking, tasks and reputation.

1379.content:
Many worlds are home to **peoples** — each with its own look, crafts, settlements and attitude to a guest. All peoples
are in the reference.

1380.content:
The people are at home in their world: the hail of their own weather (Jupiter’s mushballs, the Moon’s micrometeorites, the
Forge’s ember rain) does not hurt them, and one stuck in blocks steps out to a free spot by itself. They can still be hurt by a
blow, a fall and the visible events of a world — an eruption, a tornado, a storm’s lightning.

1381.content:
Right-click an inhabitant to open a conversation: a greeting and topics you can ask about. The **elder** tells the most:
about the people, the world and the roads.

1382.content:
Every settlement has a **chief** — the elder in its middle — and two or three **named masters**. They have their own names
(different in every settlement), a title in the window header and their own words; a crown rises above the chief's task mark,
a star above a master's. The chief gives a chain of tasks about the people's history with a reward found nowhere else; a master
gives a personal task. The people's page in the reference shows who they are.

1383.content:
Every craft speaks in its own voice and gives **work beyond trade**: a cartographer sets your compass on a place for a compass
and a fee, a master mends the item in your hand, the elder tells the history and hints at the next step of a mystery, a herder
tells you about beasts — what to feed them and how to breed them. Click an inhabitant to hear their craft (a task shows as
"Q — task"); **Shift-click** opens trading at once. With talkative inhabitants the craft is the "Tell me about your work" answer.

1384.content:
Every craft has its own trades by level — just like Earth’s villagers. The more you trade, the higher the level and the
more goods the inhabitant has.

1385.content:
A golden “**!**” overhead means the inhabitant has a job for you. Take the task in conversation, complete it — bring
something their world lacks, defeat a creature, reach a place — and hand it in. The reward is items, experience and
**reputation** with the people. Each people has fifteen to twenty tasks across its crafts; a “**?**” overhead means a task
can be handed in.

1386.content: The farmers of the tide fields: “Thalassia”.

1387.content: The inhabitants give a map to their world’s dungeon: “Dungeons and world masters”.

1388.content: In space the peoples keep stations with orders and trust: “Peoples’ stations, orders and trust”.

1390.content: The dish, the radio map and the waterfall: how to tune the receiver to signals from the sky.

1397.content:
Stars are joined with lines, seams are traced with the crosshair, vents are heard in rhythm — and radio is **tuned**. The
radio telescope shows no sky: at the top is a radio map, below it the **waterfall**: frequency left to right, time top to
bottom.

1398.content:
sits on a mast of three , and around the receiver, at its level,
a 7 × 7 dish of . The receiver shows missing blocks as ghosts, and the last block placed
assembles the dish by itself. The dish looks where it was aimed and keeps tracking that point across the sky.

1399.content:
The map is the real Galaxy: the disc and the bulge, bright sources at their real coordinates. What never rises over Earth
can be seen from the Moon or from your own station. Running machines closer than 24 blocks and thunderstorms cause
interference — put the dish away from your base. The dish does not go below 12° above the horizon: a lower source cannot be
recorded, and the beam panel tells you when it rises.

1400.content:
The sky turns in step over Earth and over the Moon. “Wow!” comes once a sidereal day for 72 seconds, when Sagittarius
crosses the meridian — at the same moment everywhere: from Earth the source stands low in the south (about 23°), from the
Moon almost overhead, and in orbit it is always in view.

1401.content: Every kind of signal has its own tuning control — the beam panel tells you which one to take, but not the solution.

1402.content: Spoiler — open the page to read

1403.content: Everyone around sees a find: the dish shoots a beam into the sky in the color of the source.

1404.content:
Almost every fast radio burst comes once. One source — in Vulpecula — repeats: once in five days it sends a series of three
to six bursts in a night (the hint “when will the signal come” counts down to it). Point the dish at Vulpecula and
straighten the arcs with the dispersion wheel.

1405.content: Spoiler — open the page to read

1406.content:
Three radio telescopes on three roads — in the Solar System, in the Interrift and in the Depths — listen as one eye once
they are tied together by hydrogen clocks. Build a  from the blueprint
() and set it beside the receiver of an assembled telescope.

1407.content:
Every four days comes the **night of Sagittarius** (a day and a half long); outside it the maser console says when the next
one begins. On the night press the maser and keep the crosshair on the drifting bright center for a minute — on every road it
moves in its own way. You get a .

1408.content: Spoiler — open the page to read

1409.content: The voice in Leo leads to a second Earth: “Thalassia”.

1410.content: From orbit the whole sky is visible: “Ships and space”.

1411.content: Radio logs feed research projects: “Station Observatory”.

1412.content: Where the navigation records lead — “Interstellar space” (behind a spoiler).

1414.content: How to find a rift in the void of the End and tear open its seam.

1419.content:
is the instrument of the dark road. It works only **in the End**, under the open sky and with
**four Eyes of Ender** in the sockets of its deck.

1420.content:
The riftscope is a multiblock: a five-by-five deck, sockets in the middle of each side, a two-block column. The journal
shows the layout. An eye goes in by using it on the socket itself — like an End portal frame. When dismantled, the eyes
drop.

1421.content:

| --------------- | ------------------------- |
| Start observing | right-click the riftscope |

1422.content:

1423.content:

| --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Tell that it is close | right at the rift the crosshair catches ripples and you hear knocking |

1427.content: A seam torn to the end opens into a rift, and the journal counts the find. All rifts are searched at once, in any order.

1428.content:
Instead of shooting stars, little **cracks** flash in the End sky — catch them to get void shards. Shards pay for a call
(the hint key, H by default): for three shards it briefly shows the nearest unfound rift and drives all the sparks toward it,
and while it sounds an arrow at the edge of the screen shows which way to turn. A found rift brings four shards — enough for
the next call.

1429.content: Beyond the rifts lie the four worlds of the dark road, reached by the shuttle. See “The roads”.

1430.content: An opened rift changes the End itself: “Nether and End changes” and “Void Shoals”.

1431.content: The worlds beyond the rifts have their own “Peoples and tasks”, “Dungeons and world masters” and “Gates”.

1432.content: A ship of the dark road goes out into the Interrift: “Ships and space” and “Places of the Interrift” (behind spoilers).

1433.content: How the road ends — “End of the Dark Road” (behind spoilers).

1435.content: Who guards the places of the Ringwrights, how to fight it, what ring sparks are for and what the Ringwright Lens shows.

1442.content:
**Watch rings** hang over the places the Ringwrights left behind. The first such place is the Monolith on the Moon; after
that, rings guard every niche with a tablet and the great places at the ends of the roads. Rings drop
, and sparks make the  — a lens that shows what the Ringwrights
left for those who look.

1443.content:
A ring of light about two blocks across, held in four clasps of dark metal. It does not roam the world: each ring keeps
a post at its place and circles a few blocks away from it. Whoever it sees, it strikes with a beam, in a cycle:

1444.content:
| Step    | How long | What you see and what to do                                                                 |
| ------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Wind-up | 1 s      | the clasps tighten, the core flares, an aiming thread reaches for you — get out of its line |

1445.content:
| Step | How long | What you see and what to do                                                                                                  |
| ---- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Beam | 1.5 s    | notched rims run from the ring to the target; the beam follows you with a lag — a step aside or a block in the way breaks it |

1446.content:
| Step    | How long | What you see and what to do                                                                            |
| ------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Cooling | 2 s      | the ring tilts and sinks, the clasps open — **it takes half again as much damage**, time for the sword |

1447.content:
**The danger sign.** A ring that has taken aim at you shows even when it is behind your back: a ring of light tightens on
the floor around your feet (under the beam it burns and ripples outward), and a line rises above the hotbar — “A watch ring
takes aim at you — step out of its beam”. The line shows over an open window too, even while you read a tablet. The sign
looks the same at every “Mod graphics” level.

1448.content:
24 health. It never follows a target farther than 26 blocks from its post; walled in by blocks, it drifts back to the
post straight through them.

1449.content:
It does not see players in Creative or spectators. With friends, each ring strikes whoever it sees itself and burns
anyone who steps into the beam.

1450.content:
The beam burns but does not push: it will not knock you off a stair or a narrow bridge. Armor soaks it like an
ordinary hit.

1451.content: It does not appear on Peaceful or with `spawn_mobs false`.

1452.content:
It does not stand on a path: over the steps of a stair (the spiral steps in the well of the Swarm Archive) or in a
passage one block wide a ring neither appears nor circles — you walk to the niche, not through it.

1453.content:
**How many**: no more than three at one place and four near one player. A place raises a new ring at most once
every 10 seconds and rests a minute or two after a ring dies — no farming sparks faster than about one a minute.

1454.content: A ring drops a  70% of the time.

1455.content: The ring’s light, curled up into a spark. It goes into:

1456.content: the  — four sparks; on an anvil a spark gives the Lens back a quarter of its charge;

1457.content:
the tier II and III modules of the far roads — one spark per recipe: interstellar drives
(, ), spindle keels
(, ) and crucible jackets
(, );

1458.content: the  — two sparks in its forge recipe;

1459.content:
Ringwright decor: the  (a ring of light on a stand, light 14) and
 (glowing seams).

1460.content: Spoiler — open the page to read

1461.content: **How to wear it**: in either hand, or over the eye — in a slot mod: the face slot of Trinkets, the head slot of Curios (NeoForge).

1462.content:
**Charge** — 1200 seconds of showing. It drains second by second only while the Lens has something to show: a place
of the Ringwrights or a hidden block within 48 blocks. It never breaks at zero — it goes dark; relight it with a ring
spark on an anvil.

1463.content:
**What you see**: at an open niche — the Ringwrights’ script right on the walls (signs you already understand in
turquoise, the rest in violet), a ring print with nine notches on the floor before the niche (up to nine blocks across; smaller in a cramped room, but never under three) and a palm
print by the opening; from afar — a trail of huge footprints toward the nearest niche, but only eight steps ahead: the
rest is yours to find. The layer washes out from you in a wave over a second and a half.

1464.content:
**For you alone**: what the Lens shows is seen only by the one looking through it — a friend beside you without a Lens
sees nothing.

1465.content: A sealed niche is smooth stone: the Lens does not give it away and spends no charge near it; open the place first.

1466.content: Spoiler — open the page to read

1467.content: Rings strike one at a time, in turn: keep an eye on the one drawing its aiming thread and hit the one that is cooling.

1468.content: A wall or pillar between you and a ring breaks its beam — there is almost always cover near a niche.

1469.content: The Lens in your off hand keeps the main hand free for the sword; over the eye it keeps both free.

1470.content: The gate rings are their work too: “Gates”.

1471.content: The great places at the ends of the roads: “End of the Dark Road” and “End of the Fire Road” (behind spoilers).

1472.content: Records that can be read only through the Lens: knots (“The Underweave”) and hallmarks (“The Underdeep”).

1474.content: Fuel, the launch pad, assembling a rocket and flying to a world you have found.

1480.content:
A world found through the telescope can be visited. Rockets come in four tiers: **lunar, interplanetary, heavy and deep
space** — each flies further than the one before.

1481.content:
— fuel: open the plant, put in coal and empty canisters (two pieces of coal fill a canister);
hoppers work with it as with a chest.

1482.content:
— charge: under the open sky by day it charges flat batteries, half a minute each.
Every flight drains one battery.

1483.content: — the launch pad; the rocket is assembled on it and does not take it along at launch.

1484.content: A battery block charges batteries from the grid of the base machines too, see “Machines and energy”.

1485.content:
Build the rocket on the pad from the bottom up — the journal shows the layout; it assembles itself once the last block
is in place (on the lunar one, the nose cone above the cabin). The layout is tied to the compass, not to the cabin: the interplanetary rocket's boosters go on the west and east sides, the fins on the north and south, and once assembled its cabin turns to face north or south. A gauge on the front of the tank shows the fuel, the lights
on the fins and the cabin windows show the charge. The tiers are told apart from afar by their silhouette: the lunar
rocket is stout, on four red fins; the interplanetary one is tall, with two boosters, a black heat-shield band and an
escape tower above the capsule; the heavy one is a thick tower on a white "skirt" of four boosters, with a checkered
section and a blunt red nose; the deep space one is a ship on five engines with spherical tanks, a habitat ring (it
spins while there is charge) and an antenna dish on top. On the heavy and deep space rockets the gauge shows helium,
and the coil rings above the nozzles glow orange.

1486.content:
Sit in the cabin and open the **star map**: you can only fly to a world found through the telescope, and only with open
sky above the rocket.

1487.content:
The rocket lands where it stood before in that world, and in a new world it looks for a flat free spot. It breaks
nothing and never lands amid lava: there is always solid ground to step out onto, and it keeps clear of the lava sea of Venus.

1488.content:
**Pack for the way back before you go.** For the chosen world the star map says what it takes to lift off from there:
fuel for the way back, a charged battery (the flight drains it, and the lunar rocket has only one), a return stage (a new world
has no launch pad, and none can be built under a landed rocket) — and landing legs: without them only the cabin comes down,
with an empty tank. Home the rocket flies the same way, back to its pad. A rocket on the pad can also be filled through pipes — by the fueling and charging
gantries.

1489.content:
A rocket has module sockets on its hull: two on the lunar rocket, three on the interplanetary, four on the heavy and six
on the deep-space rocket. Fit a module by using it on a hull socket (sneak with an empty hand to take it off), or put it
into the module slots of the cabin window. Every module shows on the rocket itself and is easy to tell from afar:

1490.content:
— two legs splayed sideways with feet, under a yellow-and-black striped housing:
the whole rocket lands, not just the cabin.

1491.content: — a little rocket on a black nozzle bell: take off from bare ground, no launch pad.

1492.content: — a crate of chest planks under an iron lid: nine slots of cargo.

1493.content: — a hump with a porthole that glows warm: room for a second passenger.

1494.content: — a barrel with a red band and fuel glowing in its sight glass: half as much fuel again.

1495.content: — a copper cabinet with two terminals and red charge bars: two more battery slots.

1496.content: — two blue wings: parked under the open sky, the rocket slowly charges itself.

1497.content: — a fan over a blue glow of air: you can breathe in the cabin and next to the landed rocket.

1498.content: — a pair of white boosters that burn in flight too: a flight costs a fifth less.

1499.content:
— a white dish with a blinking lens: after landing it tells you which way the nearest
settlement is.

1500.content:
The dark and fire roads have no rockets: the **shuttle** goes to the worlds beyond the rifts, the **bell** to the bottom
of the vents. Where the craft may go is decided by modules: the module for the next world is made from the spoils of the
previous one.
A module goes on the craft itself: click a socket on the hull with it in hand (sneak-click with an empty hand to take it
off). Every departure from the End or the Nether costs a spool of thread or an ember-tempered chain and fuel by the
world's distance, while the way back along the thread or chain is free, back to its dock or winch. A trip from world to world adds
up both distances and can exceed the tank (from the Hive to the Eye it is 12 against a tank of 10): then go home first.
The craft's console says "Ready to go" only when its supplies reach at least one found world; otherwise it says what is
missing: "Not enough liquid pearl: the nearest world takes 3".

1501.content: On the ground of another world: “Rovers”.

1502.content: Before the first launch — “Oxygen, spacesuit and climate”: you cannot breathe in the mod’s worlds.

1503.content: “Machines and energy” — where the fuel and the charge come from.

1504.content: On arrival you will find “Peoples and tasks”, “Dungeons and world masters” and “Gates”.

1505.content: The shuttle and the bell start with their own instruments: the “Riftscope” and the “Magmascope”.

1506.content: Later a ship of your own replaces the rocket: “Ships and space”.

1508.content: Ground vehicles for other worlds: three chassis, seven modules, charge, repair and the pocket capsule.

1515.content: A rover carries you, your friends and your things over another world — and folds into one item when you fly on.

1519.content:
Put a chassis, up to four modules and a  into the  (it needs no energy) and press
**Assemble**: the rover stands three blocks in front of it. Keys are those of a boat: throttle, brake and steering; sprint is a quarter
faster, jump is the handbrake. In the seat the inventory key opens the panel: the battery slot, the modules, the trunk and your own inventory.
A battery is 8,000 ⚡, and without charge the rover does not move.

1520.content: **Fold up** in the panel turns the rover with everything in it into a ; use the capsule on level ground and it unfolds.

1521.content:
Low gravity sends a rover flying off every bump, Martian dust makes it skid, the acid of Venus wears the tires: mend them with the
 (half per kit). Wheels burn in lava and crawl in water — take the Ray there.

1522.content:
| Module | What it does                  |
| ------ | ----------------------------- |
|        | 9 more cells (18 in the Mule) |

1523.content:
| Module | What it does                                               |
| ------ | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
|        | air, warmth and acid shield within 6 blocks; 30 ⚡ a second |

1524.content:
| Module | What it does                                       |
| ------ | -------------------------------------------------- |
|        | climbs two-block steps, full speed on loose ground |

1527.content:
| Module | What it does                                                         |
| ------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
|        | 5 damage to hostile creatures in sight within 14 blocks, 40 ⚡ a shot |

1528.content:
| Module | What it does         |
| ------ | -------------------- |
|        | 60 ⚡ a second by day |

1529.content:
Creatures, explosions and lava hurt the hull. Put  into the Repair slot of the panel or use one on the rover: each gives
back 4 of hull. A wrecked rover drops as a capsule with everything inside and a quarter of its hull.

1530.content: Only the owner and their `/team` drive it and open the panel; others ride as passengers. A player who leaves the game keeps the seat.

1532.content: Where to take it: “Rockets and flight”, “Ships and space”.

1534.content: The shipyard, ship forms and classes, modules, flight over a world and going out into space.

1539.content: In the cockpit: labels, zoom, picking a target

1548.content:
A ship is late-game transport. It flies over a world like a plane, climbs above the sky — and finds itself in the space
of its road, where worlds are spheres in the sky.

1549.content:
A ship is welded at the **shipyard** from parts — which ones, the form page shows. The form sets the
role (scout, freighter, warship…), the hull, hold, tank and the number of module slots. The ship’s **class** multiplies
speed, hull, hold, jump and scanner.

1550.content:
You build the shipyard yourself: the shipyard console at the middle of a long side of a 9 × 5 slipway, two crane towers of
four sections at opposite corners (the scheme and its Show in the world button are on the Shipyard page of the star journal);
clicking the console shows what is missing. The shipyard knows the scout of your road once you beat the road's first master
(Terminator Warden, Mother of the Comb, Giant's Remnant) and the hauler after the last one; other forms come from blueprints
in space caches and stations.

1551.content:
Modules go into slots: thrust, hull, hold, scanner and others, each with tiers I–III. A tier is made from the metals of
its road.

1552.content:
Over a world the ship flies like a plane: cruise, boost, turns, climb. Above the sky begins the space of the road: belts,
comets, the peoples’ stations and anomalies. A ship can be picked up into the hold by a beam, towed, and you can transfer
to another one.

1553.content:
From space a ship enters only the skies of worlds you have already been to: landed there by rocket, shuttle or bell, or
came through the gates. Earth and the small worlds are open to every pilot. At any other world the hull stops at the edge of
the sky, and the red line under the sight tells you why and what to do — for a planet, "Land here by rocket first".

1554.content:
Someone else’s ship (two players) can be refueled and mended by anyone, but only its owner takes the helm: a guest comes
aboard through the stern hatch while the owner is home, and rides as a passenger in a two-seater once the owner is in the
cockpit. Clicking such a ship says exactly that — whose it is and what it takes. Only the owner opens the ship console
(modules and hold) — from outside and from the passenger seat alike.

1555.content:
While you are aboard — as the pilot or a passenger — you are behind the hull: claws, projectiles and beams of creatures hit
the hull instead of you, at half strength. The hull does not last forever: a wrecked ship no longer shelters you. Heat, cold
and radiation are not stopped this way — those are for the suit and modules.

1556.content:
From space a ship enters a world's sky where it touches the globe — come back to Earth from the wrong side and you can land twenty
thousand blocks from your base. For free, the globe keeps the **Takeoff pad** — where the ship last left that world for space:
fly within 1500 blocks of the mark and the ship enters the sky right above it.

1557.content:
The  is help that costs resources: put it under the open sky by your base in a world you enter
from space (Earth, planets, moons, small worlds), and the ship enters the sky right above it from wherever it reaches the globe.
Only you and your team (`/team`) see it: from the ground, a beam into the sky; from space, a glint on the globe and the line
"Entering above beacon: name". By the globe the mouse wheel picks another beacon or none; the autopilot aimed at a world with a
beacon stops right above it. Up to four lit beacons per player in a world; name it in its window (right-click; the window also tells whether it is lit and why not), on an anvil or with a name tag — the name shows on the system map. Rockets do
not use it: they already land on your previous pad.

1558.content:
The beacon also works in the eight worlds beyond the End's rifts and at the bottom of Nether vents. A void or depth ship that
flies into a world's hole comes out in the sky above the chosen beacon (the mouse wheel by the hole, as by a globe), and the
Takeoff Pad mark remembers where it left through the hole. The Rift Shuttle and the Diving Bell land beside the beacon — a few
steps from the beam, not on your previous pad: they have no wheel to pick, so they take the first beacon of whoever is aboard.

1559.content:
In the Nether itself the beacon needs open space above it instead of the sky. A depth ship coming up from the Depths through
the vault surfaces in the Nether right beside your beacon, wherever it rose; without a beacon it surfaces where it dove into
the lava, if it comes up within 1500 blocks of that spot (the Takeoff Pad mark is shown on the vault). It always surfaces in
a free space big enough for the whole ship, never inside the rock; with no room anywhere near, it stays in the Depths. The
Diving Bell returning to the Nether lands on the pad it took off from.

1560.content:
**Labels in the sky.** Labels that would overlap fold into one, the most important, with “+N”: from the outskirts the
Sun shows as “Sun +19”, not two dozen names. A label hidden behind a nearby body (a ship, a boulder, a comet nucleus,
a station, a creature) fades. The **F10** key cycles labels: all → target and important → hidden. Danger signs are
always visible.

1561.content:
**Zoom.** Hold “pick block” (the mouse wheel) or your own “zoom” key in the controls: the field of view narrows like a
spyglass, and labels spread apart and grow larger. The wheel sets the power (×3, ×6, ×12), the right button the filter
(all, bodies, stations, anomalies), the left button picks a target. The card of the aimed target says what it is, how
far, and whether you can jump there — and if not, why: the ship is on a tether, not enough fuel (how much is needed and
how much is in the tank), closer than 1,500 blocks — fly there under your own power. The jump charges toward the picked
target, and the autopilot leads to it. During a jump you cannot leave the ship, even one that took off from a landing
pad: the sneak key does nothing until the ship is out of the jump.

1562.content:
**Instruments do not overlap.** Side panels (scanner, radio, anomaly steps, comet nucleus, combat) stand in columns; when
space is tight the less important one folds into a line; key hints form a column in the lower left corner.

1563.content: **Ship friends** in the console (Shift + right-click the ship) scroll with the wheel; type a name and the list filters.

1564.content:
The **F8** key (Ship: System Map in the controls) opens the **System Map**, a top-down hologram of the whole current cosmos:
bodies, orbits, asteroid belts and fields, known stations and your team. It works in the cockpit, aboard and on foot in any
cosmos; on a far road the same key opens that road's own map, and buttons lead to the Interstellar, Pattern and Section maps
if you have them.

1565.content:
**A fisheye scale**: true to size near the middle and squeezed toward the edge, so Mercury and the Kuiper belt fit in one view.
The wheel zooms toward the point under the cursor, drag to move. The rings are distances: from the Sun, from the ship (To the
ship keeps the middle on your ship) or, on foot, from you (To me); Whole system shows the whole cosmos again.

1566.content:
**Only your own finds**: the map shows only what your ship's scanner has found: stations, expedition caches, rich rocks,
fields, anomalies you noticed. Things that stay put are remembered after you leave the game; moving ones (the comet,
creatures) read "Seen N min ago" and fade after five minutes. Close marks of one kind merge into a counted heap ("Expedition
cache ×9"): click it and the map zooms in until the heap opens.

1567.content:
**Distance and time**: under the cursor, how many blocks it is from the ship (on foot, from you) and how long it takes at cruise
and at your current speed; for the target the same, plus whether you can land there and whether you can jump.

1568.content:
**Target**: click a body or mark, **Set as target**, and the **Autopilot to the target** button (from the pilot seat) flies the
ship there. The autopilot now also flies to fields, caches, rich rocks and anomalies, stopping forty blocks from their edge.

1569.content:
The scanner's **Rich rock** marks do not lie: every marked rock of a belt holds an ore heart of the ore the mark names, in its
middle, right where the mark points.

1570.content:
Jumps to a comet and to the Visitor are led: the marker stands where the target will be at the end of the jump. At a
comet you exit beyond the edge of the danger zone, at the Visitor a hundred blocks behind it, in its wake, matching its
speed.

1571.content: Spoiler — open the page to read

1572.content:
The Visitor’s disc is made of large boulders. Bring the ship over a boulder from above and match speed, without pressing
forward or up — the landing legs settle on the stone, and the ship rides along with the Visitor even with nobody aboard.
Stepping out, you stand on the boulder and can walk on it; step off the edge or jump, and the Visitor slips away from
under your feet. You cannot land on a comet: its nucleus tumbles.

1573.content:
After a scan, the comet heart shows as a marker through the ice. It is deep inside a large clump and cannot be taken by
hand: dig with the **mining beam** (left Alt) through the crust and ice. The mining beam is a ship module: it is made at a
crafting table from titanium, a lens, a coil and a battery (or traded from the Fear Drillers) and fitted into a slot of
the ship’s console.

1574.content: The anomaly steps tell you what to do with your hands, and show an instrument at the moment of the attempt.

1575.content:
**Slingshot** — pass the hole closer than 260 blocks (but not closer than 40) on boost and turn: the arc must be 50°
or more. In the sky there are rings for the 600 and 260 zones; the instrument counts the arc (“18° more”) and tells you
if you are too far or too slow. Leave the 600 zone and the maneuver counts.

1576.content:
**Ride the jet** — during an outburst enter the ring at the base of the column (the “stream entry” marker), not the red
one, and hold on in the sheath for five seconds. Where the nose points, there you are thrown — the instrument says
toward what.

1577.content:
The **Ship Friends** page of the console gives everyone an access level. Click a row to make a friend, click its label to change the level; the rows on top are
“Everyone” and your `/team`. The ship can be used while its owner is offline.

1578.content:
| Level  | What it allows                                                         |
| ------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Friend | live cargo, towing the wreck into a hold, crossing over without asking |

1579.content:
| Level     | What it allows                         |
| --------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Passenger | also comes aboard and sits without you |

1580.content:
| Level | What it allows                                                                    |
| ----- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Pilot | also flies, lands, jumps, autopilot, beacon and dock services; no console or hold |

1581.content:
| Level      | What it allows                                                                                       |
| ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| First Mate | everything you can — console, hold, hangar, upgrades — except scrapping the ship and changing rights |

1582.content:

real lines of substances — and you learn the substance, and with it the recipes made from it.

The lines are real — from the reference tables: hydrogen’s Balmer series, the sodium D lines, calcium H and K, oxygen
bands. Where the game takes liberties, the reference text says so. If a sample holds two unknown substances, you need a

to wait), or look at the Sun from a ship inside the corona with a spectrograph in hand. Its locked card in the handbook says

1688.content:
Take the race and fly to the station: a track of twelve rings of light rises around it. The clock starts at the first
ring. The next ring shines brighter than the rest and points the way on with a beam. Missing a ring does not end the race
but adds 5 seconds. Your instruments show the timer, the ring number and how far behind the station record you are. The
record (name and time) is shown on the race card at the board. A freighter makes it on the limit, a scout with time to spare.

1689.content:
At Interrift stations the rings are woven of threads, at Depths stations they are made of magma. The first race you hand
in gives the : a pennant of light flies behind your ship, a golden one for a record holder.

1690.content:
Take a convoy and fly your ship to the meeting point (a mark in the sky, 350 blocks from the station): the station’s cargo
drone comes out to meet you. The drone only moves while you are within 160 blocks and heads for a buoy 3,000–3,600 blocks
away. At one third and two thirds of the way drifters attack it, three ships first, then four. The raiders go for the cargo and
ignore your ship until you shoot at them, but every second ship of a wave is a hunter that comes straight for you. Choose whom
to shoot first: while you chase the hunter, the others wreck the drone (its hull is 120; a wave nobody drives off destroys it in
a little over a minute). Slow down as you close in: at full speed it is easy to miss the ships circling the drone. On a class B
Hornet with a single Pulse Cannon II the convoy is risky — you reach the buoy with about half your hull; on a class A ship
with Cannon III and a shield it is easy. Fall behind for more than a minute and the drone turns home, and the convoy fails. At the buoy the drone jumps, and
you can hand the order in at the board. If you own a station, its cargo drones on their runs also go under the people’s
guard. You can only escort one convoy at a time.

1699.content: The drifters’ den has no board: there is no dealing with drifters, they are only enemies.

1700.content:
**Station team.** The owner of a player station can let friends use it, with everything open to them as to the owner: modules
and tiers, the hangar, the hold, workshops, the observatory, the Zero-G Forge, the bunk and the crew; the station refinery fuels
their ships. Crouch and use an empty hand on a socket of your station to open the **Station team** window: on the left the owner
and the team (nearby, online, offline), on the right the online players you can add (type a name to search). A team holds up to
eight players and only the owner edits it; whoever is removed has the station windows closed. The same works with the mod's
command `station trust add|remove|list <player>` while standing on the station; no operator rights are needed for your own.

1701.content:
Observatory forecasts go to the whole team online, and a finished project reaches every team member. Fuel from the refinery
tanks and the free fuel at the dock go only to the owner and the team: a stranger's ship cannot drain the station.

1702.content:
**Station name.** The owner can rename the station: the pencil after the name in the title of the Station team window (Enter
saves, Esc cancels, an empty name brings back the orbit name such as "Earth-I"), or the command `station name <name>`,
`station name reset`. A name is up to 32 characters and everyone sees it: on the scanner, the System Map, the HUD and in messages.

Crouch and use an empty hand on a plug or hatch aboard: the station console opens. Choose a module, the top tier or the whole station and press **Estimate** — it shows what
comes back and what is in the way (people, ships, animals, foreign or missing blocks, things in chests and tanks). Clear it, ask again, hold
**Hold: dismantle**; for the whole station type its name first. The countdown is 5 seconds for a part and 10 for the station; leave, log out or lose the right before zero and nothing
is touched. Everyone aboard hears it and is moved to the emitter or home.

1750.content:
When you are stuck — staring at a constellation without new lines for a long time or making two mistakes in a row — the
telescope offers a hint: a plate with a key and a price. A hint reveals **one** line, and you draw it yourself. You pay
in stardust; stardust comes from shooting stars caught in the crosshair and from discoveries in the sky. In creative
mode hints are free.

1751.content:

graviscope each see further. The journal records a body you have found, and then you can fly to it. Where to look for

1763.content: Five ores and the Flame Separator

1766.content:
Thalassia is a moon of the blue giant Pontus by the orange star Hemera. You can breathe there, the water is warm, gravity is 0.9 of Earth's and a day is
20 minutes: no suit or dome is needed and ordinary crops grow. Pontus hangs high with phases, hides Hemera every noon for a few minutes and lights the nights.

1880.content:
Once a rift is open in the End, pale **void currents** in the color of that rift rise from the void at the edges of the outer
islands on its side of the sky. This is where you dive: jump with a safety line, let the currents carry you, and catch the finds
drifting in them. While the End sleeps (stage 0, see “Nether and End changes”) or the changes
are switched off, there are no currents and no finds; the main island is left alone — currents rise only by the outer islands.

1881.content:
A current stands **at an island edge**: a column from the bottom of the world up to the rim, two blocks above the ground.
Its axis slowly moves in a circle.

1882.content:
Inside a current you are lifted — faster at the axis, slower at the edge; toward the top the lift fades and you hover at the
rim while the current carries you to it. Over the ground it lets go — you step onto the island.

1883.content: **Between currents you fall.** Below 22 blocks above the bottom, the void pulls down harder than normal gravity.

1884.content: With an elytra, a current is an updraft. During Void Pull the currents are a third stronger.

1885.content: The deeper the dive, the richer the finds.

1886.content: The  is a spool of thread spun from void shards.

1892.content:

nothing: then the void keeps you. Without a line you get one warning per dive near the bottom.

1893.content: A yank is the strong moment **The line holds**; others see a sign and hear a sound.

1894.content: Left the game in mid-fall — you come back at your anchor, and no turn is spent.

has their own, and it survives leaving and a server restart.

1970.content:
The mod ships as **six files**: one per Minecraft version and loader. The game version and the loader are in the

1974.content:
All of them have the same content; install the one for your game version and loader. There is no single jar for Fabric
and NeoForge or for different game versions; on 1.20.1 the one `…-forge-…` file runs on both Forge 47 and NeoForge 47.1.
A few things look or work a little differently on 1.21.1 and 1.20.1: vanilla clouds are sparser
(that is how these versions draw them), stars in open space are a little smaller, and on NeoForge 1.21.1 and Forge 1.20.1 artifacts go only into
Curios slots. These versions have no copper nugget, so there the crusher does not break a Copper Sheet, Wiring or a Copper Coil
down into nuggets, and the Smoker Crab does not drop them. A world does not move between game versions.

1975.content:
Both files carry the mod description for their loader, so launchers and sites show the name, version and loader
by themselves. In the NeoForge mod list a second line marked “(resources)” sits next to the mod — these are its own
resources, nested in the same jar: nothing else needs installing.

1994.content:
The mod goes **both on the server and on every player’s client**: rules and state live on the server, the client draws.
The server and the players use the same file — the same loader and the same Minecraft version: a Fabric client cannot
join a NeoForge server, a 1.21.1 client cannot join a 26.3 or 1.20.1 server, and vice versa. More —
“Playing on a server”; the same page has a short part for administrators:
the mod’s command and how the mod is checked on a dedicated server.

1995.content:
**`class file version 69.0 … up to 65.0`.** The error `java.lang.UnsupportedClassVersionError: … has been compiled by a more
recent version of the Java Runtime (class file version 69.0), this version of the Java Runtime only recognizes class file
versions up to 65.0` means the game was started with an old Java: 69 is Java 25, 65 is Java 21. Minecraft 26.3 needs
**Java 25**, and it is the game itself that fails, before any mod loads (Minecraft 1.21.1 runs on Java 21, 1.20.1 on Java 17). Install Java 25 (for example from
Adoptium) and select it in your launcher’s installation settings; the official launcher and most
others pick the right Java on their own. On a server — see “The server won’t start”.

1996.content:
**Fabric: an “Incompatible mods found!” window** with the line `requires version … or later of fabric-api, which is missing`
(or `… of geckolib …`) — Fabric API or GeckoLib is not in the `mods` folder. The loader tells you what to install:
`Install geckolib, version 5.5.7 or later`.

1997.content:
**NeoForge: `requires geckolib 5.5.7 or above. Currently, geckolib is not installed`** — GeckoLib for NeoForge is not
in the `mods` folder.

2277.content: Suit modules: which for which world

2279.content: The Module Bench sets modules into sockets of the worlds’ armor and the multitool; they stay when you take the item back.

2285.content: Build the bench and press Right-click. It needs no energy.

2286.content: Put a piece of armor of the worlds or the multitool into the slot on the left: its sockets open on the panel.

2287.content: Craft a module from matter of a world on a  and click it into a free socket, or click it on the shelf of modules.

2288.content: Point at a module: you see what it gives. Take the module out the same way; take the item back — modules leave with it.

2289.content: Sockets: helmet, leggings and boots 1 each, chestplate 2; armor of later worlds — 3 in the chestplate, plates of road ends — 2 in the helmet too. Game armor has none.

2290.content: Two equal modules do not add up. A module of a set keeps silent while that set is worn whole. A heavy one takes two sockets.

2291.content: A module named for a world is weaker away from home: antigravity unit, Titan’s wings, Iris Lens, Diver’s Rudder.

2292.content: Screens (heat, cold, acid, radiation, void) cut their own kind of world harm by 35%. It is 15–45% of a blow of creatures there (none on the Moon, Venus, Mars, Facet and Forge); game armor does not stop it.

2293.content: “This item has no sockets” — it is armor of the game or the spacesuit; only armor of the worlds and the multitool fit.

2294.content: “Goes only into: …” — the module fits another part of armor; “Such a module is already fitted here” — one is enough.

2295.content: The socket is closed — a heavy module holds the next one, or the item has fewer sockets.

2300.content: One charged tool instead of picks and shovels: it mines, cuts, scans and shoots plasma.

2307.content: Charge it: in the inventory click it with a  on the cursor with the secondary (right) mouse button, +8,000 ⚡; or leave it in a charging station.

2308.content: Hold it in the main hand, hold Z: the wheel opens. Move the mouse to a mode and let go.

2309.content: “Mining” — hold Left-click on a block as with a pick: it is a pickaxe, shovel and axe at once. “Cutter” works on stone and ores 1.8 times faster for a triple charge.

2310.content: “Scanner” — press Right-click: the pulse outlines ores and loot caches around you. “Plasma” — press Right-click to shoot at creatures; the barrel heats up.

2311.content: Upgrade: craft the next version from the previous one and the core of that version — the charge and modules stay.

2312.content: Modules: put the multitool on the Module Bench and set them into sockets (Mk1 — 2, Mk2 — 3, Mk3 and Mk4 — 4).

2316.content: Shift with the Area module — one block only

2317.content: Charge holds 8,000 / 16,000 / 32,000 / 64,000 ⚡. A block costs 16–10 ⚡, the pulse 400 (a pause of 5 s), a plasma bolt 80.

2318.content: Mining level: Mk1 — iron, Mk2 — diamond, Mk3 and Mk4 — netherite. Reach is 1.5 blocks farther, scan radius 12 / 16 / 20 / 24. Never breaks.

2319.content: Plasma heats the barrel by 22–16 for a shot; at 100 it is locked for 3 s. Silk Touch and Luck do not fit together.

2320.content: Area digs 3×3 in the plane you look at, but not blocks with inventories or much harder than the middle. Charging station — 8,000 ⚡ a battery, in daylight under the sky.

2321.content: “The multitool is out of charge” — charge it: with no charge it digs nothing and does not shoot.

2322.content: “The scanner recharges” — wait for a few seconds and press Right-click again.

2323.content: Modules do nothing — they work only while the multitool is in the main hand.

2328.content: Under the open sky of Io a dose of radiation builds up; the Radiation Screen of the suit stops it entirely.

2333.content: Craft the screen from lead of Venus and hydrogen cells of Europa and put it into the chestplate of the spacesuit at the suit stand.

2334.content: Listen: a Geiger counter in the helmet clicks faster as the dose grows.

2335.content: Without a screen hide: under a roof, in a pressurized room or in the cabin of a ship the dose falls.

2336.content: To the deadly line: one minute without a suit, two in a suit. Falls within about 40 seconds under cover.

2337.content: From a quarter of the dose come weakness, then hunger, nausea and harm. The screen takes a suit socket and no charge.

2338.content: The counter clicks and it hurts — you are under the open sky: take cover first, then put on the screen.

2339.content: Suit modules: which for which world

2342.content: In the thick air of Titan a person flies on muscles alone; elsewhere the wings stay folded.

2348.content: Break the pale evaporite on the shores of Titan for benzene cocrystal, bake it into polymer sheets and stretch them on a titanium frame.

2349.content: Put the wings in the chestplate slot over the spacesuit.

2350.content: Jump and press Space in the air: they open. Press Space again to flap — up and forward.

2351.content: Glide between flaps and land on the ground.

2352.content: A flap costs some hunger (ten — about half a drumstick); they come at most every 0.6 s.

2353.content: Wings wear out like elytra; a polymer sheet in the other hand mends a third of their strength with Right-click.

2354.content: “The air here is too thin for the wings” — they open only on Titan.

2357.content: Armor of the worlds is worn in the usual slots over the spacesuit, has sockets and a set bonus.

2362.content: Craft the pieces from materials of the world — in chests there is none.

2363.content: Hold G over a piece: it tells the strength of the set, its flaw and what two and four pieces give.

2364.content: Wear all four for the full gift. Against heat, cold, acid, radiation or void of a world put screens into sockets.

2365.content: Every set has a real flaw — slower steps or blows, thin plates, fire, frost or light that hurts more, lightning that seeks you: read the tooltip.

2366.content: Repair with the ore of its world on an anvil or with a plate of the mod in the other hand.

2367.content: Creatures still hurt much — part of the blow is world harm: each piece stops 3–17% of it, best of its own kind; add screens and suit modules.

2371.content: An artifact is a ring, pendant or belt that works while it is worn in a slot of Trinkets or Curios.

2376.content: Install Trinkets (Fabric) or Curios/Trinkets (NeoForge): the mod works without it, but artifacts cannot be worn.

2377.content: Craft it or find it in the chests of dungeons; the tooltip says the slot — ring, pendant or belt.

2378.content: Open your inventory, click the slot of the mod and put the artifact in: its effect starts at once.

2379.content: Hold G over it to read everything it does and where to get it.

2380.content: It works only while worn in its slot and only for the wearer; two of the same kind do not help twice.

2381.content: One of them is worn on the back; a compass of signals is used in the hand.

2382.content: “To wear it, install a slot mod” — no Trinkets or Curios is installed (or it is for another loader).

2385.content: Weapons of the worlds have an ability and grow with you: every kill raises their mastery.

2391.content: Make a weapon at a crafting table from what a world and its creatures give; some lie in dungeon chests, and hearts of masters make their own.

2392.content: Hold G over the item in any window with slots: a screen shows the model, numbers, mastery levels and where to get it.

2393.content: Take it in the main hand: some abilities fire on Right-click, others on a hit; the tooltip says which and how long they recharge.

2394.content: Kill hostile creatures with it in the main hand: each gives experience by its health. The level-up line says what is new.

2395.content: Right-click — the ability of a weapon with one

2397.content: Mastery has five levels; experience is the health of the victim divided by five, at least 1. Peaceful animals give nothing.

2398.content: Mastery lives in the item itself and goes with it from hand to hand.

2399.content: A recharge starts only when the ability has worked.

2400.content: Nothing happens on Right-click — the ability needs a hit, is recharging or has no target: read the tooltip.

2404.content: How to use everything in the mod: steps, keys, conditions.

2416.content: How to use the machines, instruments, vehicles and places of the mod: numbered steps, keys, conditions and limits, and what to do when it does not work. These are the same pages as in the game: the Manual tab of the star journal, or hold G over an item in any window. Keys are named by their defaults — in the game the pages show your own.

2417.content: Observatory building set — Decorative blocks for a telescope house.

2418.content: Star Journal — The journal keeps your path: what to do next, how it is done, and everything you have found.

2419.content: Polished Lens — Optical parts: every telescope and many instruments start with a polished lens.

2420.content: Refractor Telescope — The first telescope: the Moon, Mars and the brightest constellations.

2421.content: Looking through a telescope — The sky itself changes while you look: turn your head, join stars into constellations and focus on planets.

2422.content: Reflector Telescope — The second telescope: zooms 3 times and shows the planets up to Jupiter.

2423.content: Astrograph and graviscope — Two telescopes too heavy for a tripod: they stand on a base of blocks.

2424.content: Magmascope — Listens to the magma under the Nether and finds vents — roads to four worlds.

2425.content: Reading a spectrum — Burns a sample and shows the lines of its substances; what you know opens recipes and instruments.

2426.content: Spectrograph: light of the Sun and worlds — Catches the light of the sky for the same puzzle as in the laboratory: what is the air there made of.

2427.content: Ore Scanner — Shows veins of ores whose standard you have recorded in the laboratory.

2428.content: Unknown samples and weak spots — Finds that open in the laboratory, and parts of creatures that tell how to hit them harder.

2429.content: Building a radio telescope — Hears what no eye sees, by day and in rain, on Earth, on the Moon and in open space.

2430.content: Radio signals: four instruments — Every kind of signal is tuned with its own instrument, and the line under the map hints which.

2431.content: Rare signals: series and Pontus — Two signals that come by the clock: the way to a magnetar and to Thalassia.

2432.content: Interferometer of three roads — Three radio telescopes on three roads make one night’s image of the Galactic Center.

2433.content: Riftscope — Looks into the void of the End and finds rifts — the ways to four worlds.

2434.content: First power grid — From the first generator to a machine that runs: touching blocks and beams of light.

2435.content: Coal Generator — Burns anything a furnace burns and turns it into energy.

2436.content: Machine sides and redstone — Where hoppers, pipes and energy enter and leave a machine, and how to switch it off.

2437.content: Solar Panel — Energy from daylight, without fuel.

2438.content: Battery block — Stores spare energy and gives it back; charges portable batteries for rockets.

2439.content: Induction Emitter — Powers every machine in a ball around it without beams.

2440.content: Entangled Resonator — Carries energy between two bases at any distance, even between worlds.

2441.content: Energy converter and other mods — A bridge between the beam grid and cables and machines of other mods.

2442.content: Gravity Generator — Sets the gravity you choose in a ball around it.

2443.content: Machine versions and cards — A higher version works faster and holds more; a card changes one thing.

2444.content: Multimeter and manometer — Show what is going on in the beam grid and in the pipes.

2445.content: Crusher — Two dusts from one raw ore; glass, salt and fuel from the rock of other worlds.

2446.content: Melt Pump — Draws metal and crystals out of molten seas and lakes.

2447.content: Flame Separator — Burns Hemera oil to turn raw Thalassian ore into the ore of home you choose.

2448.content: Fuel plant — Rocket fuel from coal and helium-3 from regolith. It needs no energy.

2449.content: Charging station and batteries — Charges portable batteries and the multitool from the sun.

2450.content: Fuel Depot — Stores one liquid fuel and shares it through fuel pipes.

2451.content: Liquids and buckets — Where each liquid comes from, how to take it and what to do with it.

2452.content: Pearl Liquefier — Melts ender pearls into liquid pearl, the fuel of the rift shuttle.

2453.content: Cryo Still — Turns ice and magma cream into coolant, the fuel of the diving bell.

2454.content: How machines work — What every machine has in common: energy, sides, hoppers, redstone, upgrades.

2455.content: Electric Furnace — Smelts everything a furnace smelts, twice as fast and without coal.

2456.content: Bioreactor — Turns plants into oxygen: the first source of air for a base and a suit.

2457.content: Electrolyzer — Splits water into oxygen and rocket fuel hydrogen, and draws oxygen out of the ground where there is no ice.

2458.content: Sealed room and airlock — A room full of air on any world: breathe without a suit, with no heat, cold or acid.

2459.content: Oxygen Dome — Holds a ball of air without walls: breathe, plant saplings, keep a respawn bed.

2460.content: Acid Scrubber — Keeps the air of Venus and the Breath from eating you around a base. It gives no oxygen.

2461.content: Hydroponic Bed — Grows crops without soil, water, air or light — and closes the circle of air on a base.

2462.content: Suit Rack — Sets modules into the torso of the suit and fills it with oxygen and charge.

2463.content: Suit modules: which for which world — Four sockets of the torso decide how long and where you live.

2464.content: Spacesuit and oxygen — Without air and a whole suit you live seconds in another world.

2465.content: Storage: terminal and cells — All your things in one window with search and sorting.

2466.content: Crafting from the storage — A crafting grid in the storage window: parts come from the storage.
